article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Elsinore and La Bola Negra collected key awards for the audience favorite and jury pick for top narrative feature, respectively at the just-concluded 34th edition of the Hamptons Film Festival .

La Bola Negra was selected as the Best Narrative Feature at the fest, which ran October 2 to 12. The film, directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, is Spain’s official submission for the Best International Feature Film category at the upcoming Oscars. It emerged from the Toronto Film Festival with heat after winning the TIFF People’s Choice award , often an Oscar bellwether.

Related Stories

‘La Bola Negra’ Review: Spain’s Javier Calvo And Javier Ambrossi Capture Hearts With Their Unashamedly Romantic Decades-Spanning Drama – Cannes Film Festival

‘Elsinore’ Review: Andrew Scott Is Heartbreakingly Great As AIDS-Stricken Star Determined To Play ‘Hamlet’ – Telluride Film Festival

Another hopeful with a presence at the Hamptons is Elsinore , which made its East Coast premiere at the event. Directed by Simon Stone, the film starring Andrew Scott won the international people’s choice award at Toronto, along with prizes at other festivals in recent weeks.

Watch on Deadline

Because of its timing in between larger fall festivals and the surge of campaign season later in the year, the Hamptons has built a reputation as a fest of note. It doesn’t hurt that it takes place near the beaches of Long Island’s East End about 90 miles from New York City, long a vacation destination and a place to see and be seen. This year’s edition featured more than 140 feature films and shorts.

NAZA , which has drawn packed screenings and ovations but also protests and controversy for its documentary portrait of Israeli military attacks on Palestinian communities, also collected an award. The film, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, received the Victor Rabinowitz & Joanne Grant Award for Social Justice. The film recognizes a film that exemplifies the values of peace, equality, global justice and civil liberties.

Burgundy , directed by Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw, captured HIFF’s documentary audience award.

La Bola Negra was described in a statement by HIFF Narrative Competition jury members Cara Cusumano, Jeremy O. Harris and David Rooney as a “triptych of queer desire, queer memory and queer resistance weaves together an epic story using revisionist history and builds to an emotional climax that rips to the core.”

The narrative jury also gave a Special Mention to The Guest , which is directed by Mads Mengel.

Best Documentary Feature honors went to If Pigeons Turned to Gold . Documentary Competition Jury members Carlos A. Gutiérrez, Mark Obenhaus and Sky Sitney called it “a bold, deeply personal story of the filmmaker’s own family struggles with addiction. It is told with provocative rawness and inventiveness.”

Other HIFF honors included the Junior Jury Award, from a panel of East Hampton High School students, given to Mouse ; the Artemis Rising Foundation Raise the Vibration Award for Social Impact, to The Drug in Our Pocket and A Song for the Snow Lion ; the Peter Macgregor-Scott Memorial Award, to Laser-Gato ; the Sherzum Award, for films tackling LGBTQ+ people, issues and concerns, to What Will I Become? and Welcome to Paris ; the Brizzolara Family Foundation Award for Films of Conflict & Resolution to The Choice ; the Suffolk County Next Exposure Grant to Barbizon ; and the Zelda Penzel “Giving Voice to the Voiceless” Award, to Wild Inside .

Ben’Imana and The Drug in Our Pocket won the documentary and narrative categories, respectively, of the New York Women in Film & Television’s awards for excellence.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "乡村性：省级摄影收藏", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该项目已获得法国文化部授予的“摄影诞生二百周年”标签，并成为该周年官方日程的一部分，展期为2026年9月1日至2027年9月30日。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "二百年前，在勃艮第诞生了一种新图像，被视为第一张照片：尼谢弗尔·涅普斯（Nicéphore Niepce，1765–1833）的《鸽子窝风景》。当我们今天习惯于不断用手机捕捉影像时，我们必须体认到尼谢弗尔·涅普斯坚持不懈的独创精神对我们生活产生的深远影响。因此，第一张照片是一个风景，透过窗户望去，被定格在锡版上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在热尔省，乡村景观构成了我们日常生活的心脏。在该省，农业依然占据主导地位——近年来，这一主题已成为重大的社会议题——弗拉朗省立遗产中心一直致力于通过摄影媒介将乡村生活置于其关注的核心。源于与摄影师丹尼尔·梅涅（Daniel Maigné）的一次相遇，名为《田野深度》（La profondeur des champs）的年度系列展览已经持续了15年以上。每位受邀的摄影师都规划了各自的“历程”，并对这一主题提出了自己的视角。首届展览自然献给加斯科涅；随后，其视野扩大到法国的乡村生活，进而延伸至欧洲乃至更广阔的世界。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一个省级摄影收藏已经汇集，作为国家摄影诞生二百周年盛大庆祝活动的一部分，我们希望向公众呈现这一探索本地及其他地区乡村生活主题的摄影之旅。共有17位男女摄影师参展，每个人都有其独特的视角，使观众能够探索各种相互贯穿的表现形式，涵盖纪录片、艺术或私密方法，并运用不同的技术（从胶片到数码、从老式相机到智能手机、从黑白到彩色）……", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这场回顾展呈现了各自独特的宇宙，但依然突显了串联每场展览的共同主线，例如对农民劳作姿态与场景的描绘，以及人类活动对景观的影响。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为展览的序曲，为了缅怀摄影的早期岁月，皮埃尔·门杜斯（Pierre MENDOUSSE，1870–1933）的照片将进行展出。作为一名教师和“业余”摄影师，他在20世纪之交记录了热尔省的生活，特别是在西莫尔的生活，同时始终保持着对世界的开放视野。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2026年10月20日至2027年3月21日", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "https://www.patrimoine-musees-gers.fr/le-bicentenaire-de-la-photographie/", "links": [{"text": "https://www.patrimoine-musees-gers.fr/le-bicentenaire-de-la-photographie/", "url": "https://www.patrimoine-musees-gers.fr/le-bicentenaire-de-la-photographie/"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
Rurality(ies): the departmental photographic collection

This project has been awarded the ‘Bicentenary of Photography’ label by the Ministry of Culture and forms part of the official programme for the Bicentenary, running from September 1st 2026 to September 30th 2027.

Two hundred years ago, in Burgundy, a new image was born, regarded as the first photograph: ‘View from Le Gras’ by Nicéphore Niepce (1765–1833). We must appreciate the impact that Nicéphore Niepce’s persistent ingenuity has had on our lives, at a time when we are constantly capturing images with our mobile phones. The first photograph was, therefore, a landscape, viewed from a window, fixed onto a tin plate.

In the Gers, the rural landscape lies at the heart of our daily lives. In this department, where agriculture still predominates – a subject that has become a major social issue in recent years the Departmental Heritage Centre in Flaran has sought to place rural life at the centre of its focus through the medium of photography. Stemming from a meeting with the photographer Daniel Maigné, an annual series of exhibitions entitled *La profondeur des champs* ( the depth of field) has been running for over 15 years. Each guest photographer charts his/her own ‘course’ and offers his/hers perspective on this subject. The first edition was, of course, dedicated to Gascony; the scope then broadened to rural life in France, then Europe and the wider world.

A departmental photographic collection has been assembled, and it is this photographic journey exploring the theme of rural life here and elsewhere that we wish to present to the public as part of the large national celebration of the Bicentenary of Photography. Seventeen photographers, both men and women, are represented, each with their own unique perspective, allowing visitors to explore a wide variety of expressions linked by a common thread ranging from documentary, artistic or intimate approaches, and using different techniques (from film to digital, from vintage cameras to smartphones, from black and white to colour), …

The retrospective, with its unique worlds, nevertheless highlights the common thread linking each exhibition such as the depiction of the gestures and settings of peasant labour and the impact of human activity on the landscape.

As a prelude to this exhibition, recalling the early days of photography, prints by Pierre MENDOUSSE (1870–1933) will be on display. A teacher and ‘amateur’ photographer, he documented life in the Gers region particularly in Simorre at the turn of the twentieth century, whilst maintaining an open outlook on the world.

From October 20th 2026 to March 21st 2027

title_original: Collector’s Diary: Chang Osathanugrah Reflects on What It Means to See Art with Fresh Eyes After Years of Looking
editorial_title_zh: 收藏家日记：昌·奥萨塔努格拉（Chang Osathanugrah）反思在多年观展后以全新目光审视艺术的意义
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这位“顶级200位收藏家”撰文回忆了他在香港看到的一件令他念念不忘的作品，以及Dib曼谷美术馆开馆第一年的经历。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "我从未想过一只会说话的青蛙能让我重新记起自己当初为何会爱上当代艺术，我也绝对没想到在有机会买下它之前就错过了它。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "三月里，正值一段凉爽的天气，这让我想起为什么我依然喜爱香港——尽管它已不再完全是我记忆中的那个地方。在巴塞尔艺术展香港展会（Art Basel Hong Kong）的埃丝特·施佩尔（Esther Schipper）画廊展位上，我偶遇了瑞安·甘德（Ryan Gander）2025年的雕塑作品《你完整了我，或者我看到了你看不见的东西（青蛙的故事）》（You Complete Me, or I see things you can’t see (A Frog’s Tale)）。在这件超现实作品中，一只栖息在盆栽植物上的超写真青蛙发出了一个小女孩的声音，其台词在纯真而又诡异深邃的存在主义沉思洪流中流转。这就像是走进了一个真正懂得人类本质的童话故事。画廊经办人带着面对抱有希望的收藏家时特有的温和语气传达了一个消息：这件作品已经无法购买。事实证明，已经有人把这只青蛙收入囊中了。我早就对将作品拱手让给其他收藏家这件事释怀了，但失去这件作品带来的痛感比以往任何一次都要深刻。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在得知我无法拥有它之前，这件作品所做的事是打破了一种我已开始习惯将其视为平常的疲惫感，而且我深信这种疲惫感并非我一人独有。称之为艺博会疲惫症，或是某种更接近低调的艺术界不适感；这两种诊断感觉都很贴切，我猜那周有一半的会展中心都在忍受着同一种未确诊的病症。有那么几分钟，我没有去想价格、出处、市场周期，或者一件作品在艺术家创作生涯中处于什么位置。我什么也没有评估。我只是在单纯地观看，就像我小时候那样。那种眩晕般的感受从那时起一直留存至今。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一点小小的安慰，甘德的作品已经进入了Dib曼谷美术馆的馆藏。这家私立美术馆是我父亲毕生的梦想，我们在他去世两年后的2025年底将其开馆。在美术馆开幕之前，我们购入了甘德的《未触及的理念机器》（Untouched Idea Machines, 2025）。这是一个壁挂式黄铜出签器，只需按一下按钮，就能打印出大约2,000个未实现的艺术创作构想之一。我们计划在今年秋天的第二场展览中展出它。在这种情况下，带着一个构想而不是一只青蛙回家似乎再合适不过了。", "links": [{"text": "Dib Bangkok", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/dib-bangkok/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Collectors_Diary_Ver2.jpg?w=400", "alt": "复合图像显示：特瑞尔的天空景观；夹在三块岩石之间的两面镜子的雕塑；一个人从黄铜板上抽取门票；以及将光线反射到地板上显现出阴影的装置。", "caption": "按顺时针方向从左上角起：詹姆斯·特瑞尔（James Turrell）《直上》（Straight Up），2025年；阿丽莎·科德（Alicja Kwade）《小三重藏匿》（Little Triple Be-Hide），2023年；瑞安·甘德《理念机器》（Idea Machine），2024年；以及保罗·陈（Paul Chan）《第二道光》（2nd Light），2006年，均由Dib曼谷美术馆收藏。按顺时针方向从左上角起：摄影：Watcharapong Sermwichitchai/由Dib曼谷美术馆提供；由纽约佩斯画廊提供/©Alicja Kwade；摄影：Andrea Rossetti/©2025 Ryan Gander and VG Bild-Kunst, Bonn/Courtesy Esther Schipper, Berlin, Paris, Seoul；由上海BANK/MABSOCIETY画廊提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这也是我一段时间以来出行最少的一年：事实证明，商业责任有着它自身的引力，今年让我切实地留在了曼谷，只有过几次短暂的香港、上海和新加坡之行，其中包括在Art SG艺博会上就当今美术馆建设责任发表的小组讨论。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "四月下旬的上海之行名义上是为了在老法租界太仓路的一间贵宾室（viewing room）为一屋子企业家举办一场《Monocle》讲座，不过真正的吸引力在于那里正在考虑纳入Dib馆藏的一系列保罗·陈（Paul Chan）作品，其中包括《第二道光》（2nd Light, 2006）。作为陈“七光”（Seven Lights）系列的一部分，这件如今已有20年历史的装置作品仅凭光线就让树木、旗帜和坠落人物的阴影在地板上漂移，使整个展室呈现出一种美感与脆弱性共存的梦境特质。我意识到，光线可以像颜料或青铜一样具有表现力，而这件作品仅仅要求我在这种超出舒适区的不确定性中多停留一会儿，这或许更接近体验艺术本该有的样子。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管如此，我依然不断回到一个问题，这也是Dib的核心指导原则：深度在哪里与可及性相遇？一件经过深思熟虑的作品，能否在保持其思想丰厚奖赏的同时，依然能够与初次接触它的人产生共鸣？我不认为这两个世界像我们倾向于认为的那样相距甚远。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "今年看着成千上万名初次来访的观众走过Dib，更加印证了这一点。经验丰富的收藏家并不一定比初学者看到更多；我们只是知道得更多，而这并不是同一回事。孩子们很少会问一件作品属于哪个流派。他们会问为什么它感觉充满生命力，或者为什么它看起来如此奇特。如果我们纵容它，专业知识就会压倒惊叹。面临的挑战不是学习更多关于艺术的知识。而是重新学会如何去观看它。这确实是我过去几个月里一直在思考的个人问题：在观看了这么多年艺术之后，一个人究竟该如何保持以新鲜的目光去看待它？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "遗憾的是，我今年不得不缺席威尼斯双年展；事务将我留在了曼谷。但我们的总监美和子（Miwako Tezuka）代表Dib前往，回来时谈起了洛娜·辛普森（Lorna Simpson）在雷东多宫（Punta della Dogana）举办的展览“第三者”（Third Person）——这是同为“顶级200位收藏家”的弗朗索瓦·皮诺（François Pinault）在威尼斯的两个展览空间之一。最让美和子震撼的是《堆叠的石头/振动的循环》（Stacked Stones/Vibrating Cycles, 2020），这是一件顶部饰有颂钵的堆叠石头装置，观众应邀可以亲自敲响它们。她说，从其中升起的音调呼应了已故艺术家蒙天·布恩玛（Montien Boonma）将艺术视为实践而非奇观的观点，温和地敦促人们以谦逊战胜傲慢。听到关于这件作品的描述，我的错失恐惧症（FOMO）真实无比。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "美和子说，当她自己敲响那些钵时，她还从这些钵中带走了一些别的东西，一种熟悉而亲近的感觉。她说，这是她一整年里体验到的、最接近我们首展一直想要触及的东西。“（隐）显在”（(In)visible Presence）以记忆为核心：我已故的父亲、我的祖父、布恩马的作品，以及早在该机构成立之前就让 Dib 成为现实的核心群体。这是一个肃穆的展览，从不要求任何人对失落视而不见，而是试图将体验失落意味着什么具体呈现出来。从本质上讲，这是一首关于精神和解的颂歌。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们的第二场展览“给予生命”（Giving article_text:
I hadn’t expected a talking frog to remind me of why I fell in love with contemporary art, and I certainly hadn’t expected to lose it before I ever had the chance to buy it.

In March, during a stretch of cool weather that reminds me why I still love Hong Kong, even when it no longer feels quite like the place I remember, I came across Ryan Gander’s 2025 sculpture You Complete Me, or I see things you can’t see (A Frog’s Tale) at Esther Schipper’s booth at Art Basel Hong Kong. In the surreal work, a hyperreal frog perched in a potted plant speaks in the voice of a young girl, whose dialogue moves through a stream of existential musing, both innocent and eerily profound. It was like entering a fairy tale that understood something true about being human. The gallerist delivered the news with the gentleness reserved for a hopeful collector: the work was not available. Someone else, it turned out, had already claimed the frog. I have long made peace with losing works to other collectors, but losing this one cut deeper than past ones had.

What the piece did, before I learned I couldn’t have it, was interrupt a fatigue I had begun to accept as ordinary, and one I doubt is mine alone. Call it art fair fatigue, or something closer to a low-key art world malaise; either diagnosis feels apt, and I suspect half the convention center that week was nursing the same undiagnosed condition. For a few minutes, I was not thinking about price, provenance, market cycles, or where a work sat within the artist’s practice. I was not evaluating anything at all. I was simply looking, the way I did as a child. That giddy feeling has stayed with me since.

As a small consolation, Gander is already in the collection of Dib Bangkok , the private museum that was my father’s lifelong dream and that we opened at the end of 2025, two years after his death. Ahead of the museum’s inauguration, we acquired Gander’s Untouched Idea Machines (2025), a wall-mounted brass dispenser that prints out one of some 2,000 unrealized ideas for artworks at the press of a button. We plan to put it on view in our second show this fall. Under the circumstances, it seemed only fitting to go home with an idea rather than a frog.

This was also one of the least traveled years I have had in some time: business responsibilities, it turns out, have their own gravity, and this year has kept me literally grounded in Bangkok, with only brief trips to Hong Kong, Shanghai, and Singapore, including a panel at Art SG on the responsibilities of building museums today.

A Shanghai trip came in late April, ostensibly for a Monocle talk to a room of entrepreneurs, though the real draw was at a viewing room on Taicang Road, in the old French Concession, where a series of Paul Chan works were being considered for Dib’s collection, including 2nd Light (2006). A part of Chan’s “Seven Lights” series, this now 20-year-old installation features shadows of trees, flags, and falling figures drifting across the floor in light alone, the room taking on the quality of a dream where beauty and fragility coexist. Light, I realized, can be as expressive as pigment or bronze, and this work asked only that I dwell a little longer in the uncertainty than felt comfortable, which is perhaps closer to what experiencing art should be.

Still, I keep returning to one question, and a guiding one for Dib: Where does depth meet accessibility? Can a deeply considered work remain intellectually rewarding while still speaking to someone encountering it for the very first time? I do not believe those two worlds are as far apart as we tend to assume.

Watching thousands of first-time visitors move through Dib this year has only confirmed it. Experienced collectors don’t necessarily see more than beginners; we simply know more, and that is not the same thing. Children rarely ask what movement a work belongs to. They ask why it feels alive, or why it seems strange. Expertise can overwhelm wonder if we allow it to. The challenge is not learning more about art. It is remembering how to look at it. That really has been the personal question for me these past months: How does one keep seeing art with fresh eyes after so many years of looking at it?

Sadly, I had to forego the Venice Biennale this year; business kept me in Bangkok. But our director Miwako Tezuka went on Dib’s behalf and came back talking about Lorna Simpson’s exhibition, “Third Person” at Punta della Dogana, one of two Venice exhibition spaces of fellow Top 200 Collector François Pinault. What struck Miwako most was Stacked Stones/Vibrating Cycles (2020), an installation of stacked stones crowned with singing bowls that visitors are invited to sound themselves. The tones rising off it, she said, echoed the late artist Montien Boonma’s view of art as practice rather than spectacle, gently urging humility over hubris. Hearing about that piece, my FOMO was very real.

Miwako said she took something else away from the bowls when she sounded them herself, something close to home. She said it was the closest thing she’d experienced all year to something our first show had been reaching for. “(In)visible Presence” was built around memory: my late father, my grandfather, Boonma’s work, and the core community of people who made Dib possible long before the institution existed. It was a somber show that never asked anyone to look away from loss but tried instead to embody what it means to experience loss. In essence, it was an ode to spiritual reconciliation.

“Giving Life,” our second exhibition, will mark the moment we finally allow ourselves to celebrate again. Featuring around 30 artists, including Alexander Calder, Rirkrit Tiravanija, and Izumi Kato, the show explores the many ways artists breathe new life into materials, objects, and ideas. What fascinates me most is how some begin with things that already carry their own histories: spent bomb shells, living plants, old machinery. Objects shaped by conflict, time, or everyday use are transformed into something unexpectedly alive. Many of these works were made while their countries were at war, their economies were collapsing, or authoritarian governments were tightening their grip on the freedoms that make life feel like your own person. Yet together they make a quiet but unmistakable case for life itself. That feels worth celebrating. Perhaps this abundance of life is my own response to the undiagnosed malaise I carried home from art fairs. Whatever it is, it already seems to be working.

Away from museums, the market has continued its own reckoning over the past year. The top of the auction world and the prices for historical artists kept climbing while blue-chip, middle-market names looked shakier: a natural cycle, it seems to me. In other news, and to my joy, René Magritte deservedly became one of the market’s most sought-after names, proof that quality paired with scarcity only boosts appetite. This past June, Sotheby’s London sold La Belle Promenade (1965) for $21.6 million, while the house’s Paris branch sold La Magie Noire (1934) for $12.3 million in October 2025.

The subtle painterly quality that draws me to Magritte also brings me much closer to home, to the paintings of Prae Pupityastaporn, whose work I have collected for almost a decade. A visit in early June to Sutima Sucharitakul’s Nova Contemporary in Bangkok’s Samyan-Rama4 area deepened my appreciation of her work. Pupityastaporn takes ordinary subjects—a window or a landscape, for example—and suspends them in a real yet eerie, quietly humming dreamscape, softer and more interior than Magritte’s. There is a silent magic within the mundanity in her work that reminds me that within our everyday lives there is actually something quite sublime. It’s this quality that makes her one of Thailand’s most exciting and unique painters.

Right now, there is a generational story unfurling. The children of collectors (myself excluded, having apparently missed the rebellious gene) do not always wish to inherit their parents’ taste, and I understand the instinct, even if I never quite felt it myself. Someone actually complained to me not long ago that their parents had bought a Monet. I digress. Yes, it’s hard to watch, though I suspect what’s really at stake has less to do with taste than with the relationship between parent and child, playing itself out through whatever does or doesn’t end up on the walls at home.

Nonetheless, I’ve been feeling unusually optimistic about Thailand this year. It seems to me that a newer style of gallery, built more around community and vibe, is answering that gap. It feels like its own coming-of-age story is still being written. Bangkok Kunsthalle, for example, continues to push forward in Yaowarat; the Jim Thompson Art Center is still building on the momentum Gridthiya (Jeab) Gaweewong created there; and Central Group’s deCentral, led by my old schoolmate Punn Chirakiti, opens next year. Moreover, there seems to be a growing wave of new collectors and patrons entering Bangkok’s cultural scene. Together, they’ve kept me far more entertained close to home than any frog in the bustle of an art fair ever managed. None of it is mine to take credit for, which is perhaps why it has been such a pleasure simply to watch it unfold.

Being grounded at home, as it turned out, wasn’t so bad. It gave me an excuse to sit still and reflect. Collecting has taught me a great deal over the years. Going back to Gander’s frog, I’m reminded that art is not something we are necessarily meant to fully understand. The works that remain with us are rarely the ones we can completely explain. They are the ones that change how we see the world and, every so often, remind us how to see it at all.
excerpt_original: The Top 200 Collector writes about a work he saw in Hong Kong that stuck with him and the first year of Dib Bangkok.

解説・あらすじ

ドキュメンタリー映画監督・金聖雄が、「SAYAMA みえない手錠をはずすまで」「袴田巖 夢の間の世の中」「獄友」「オレの記念日」に続いて撮りあげた「冤罪」シリーズ第5弾。無罪が確定した袴田事件の袴田巖さんと姉・ひで子さん、いまだ再審裁判の扉が開かない狭山事件の石川一雄さんと妻・早智子さんの15年を記録し、ふたつの事件の「うそ」と「ほんと」に迫る。 2024年9月26日に無罪判決を受けた袴田巖さんと、第3次再審請求中の2025年3月11日に無念のまま亡くなった石川一雄さん。石川さん夫妻との出会いから冤罪をテーマにした映画を撮り続けてきた金監督が、権力にあらがい前を向いて歩み続けるふたつの家族にカメラを向ける。理不尽を強いられながらも、おおらかな心で生きる彼らのささやかな日常を通して、日本の司法の残酷さを浮き彫りにしていく。 俳優の北村有起哉が語りを担当。

article_text:
This November, Aperture will release Josef Koudelka: Invasion Prague 68 in a hardcover format.

When Soviet-led troops invaded Czechoslovakia in August 1968, ending the short-lived Prague Spring, Josef Koudelka was one of the first on the scene. As an acclaimed theater photographer, Koudelka (born in Moravia, Czechoslovakia, 1938) knew nothing about photojournalism, but that would soon change. In the turmoil of the invasion, he took a series of photographs purely for himself, which were miraculously smuggled out of the country. A year after they reached New York, Magnum Photos distributed and credited the photos to an unknown Czech photographer. Their significance earned the still-anonymous photographer the Robert Capa Award. Sixteen years would pass before Koudelka could safely acknowledge authorship.

This hardcover edition of Invasion Prague 68 contains 250 images selected by Koudelka from his archive, punctuated by contemporary broadcasts and eyewitness accounts. Almost sixty years later, these searing photographs return to light, standing as a timely reminder of the brutality of political repression and the importance of bearing witness to injustice.

Aperture would like to thank the Institute of Contemporary History at the Academy of Sciences of the Czech Republic, Prague, and Magnum Photos, Paris, for their assistance in publishing this book. Josef Koudelka: Invasion Prague 68 is published by Aperture and available at aperture.org .

About Josef Koudelka Josef Koudelka (born in Moravia, Czechoslovakia, 1938; naturalized French, 1987) began his career as an aeronautical engineer before turning full-time to photography in the late 1960s. In 1968 he photographed the Soviet-led invasion of Czechoslovakia. In 1969, he was anonymously awarded the Overseas Press Club’s Robert Capa Gold Medal for the photographs that were published with the initials P.P. (Prague photographer). Koudelka left Czechoslovakia seeking political asylum, in 1970, and shortly thereafter joined Magnum Photos. His awards include the Prix Nadar, Grand Prix National de la Photographie, HCB Award, Hasselblad Foundation International Award in Photography, Medal of Merit from the Czech Republic, and being named Commandeur de l’Ordre des Arts et des Lettres by the French Ministry of Culture. Significant exhibitions of his work have been held at the Museum of Modern Art and International Center of Photography, New York; Hayward Gallery, London; Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam; and Palais de Tokyo, Paris. Koudelka’s books include Gypsies (1975), Exiles (1988), Black Triangle (1994), Chaos (1999), Invasion 68: Prague (2008), Wall (2013), Ruins (2020), and Next (by Melissa Harris, 2023). He is based in Paris and Prague.

About Aleš Najbrt Aleš Najbrt studied typography and book design with Jan Solpera at the Academy of Arts, Architecture, and Design, Prague. He was an art director of the influential Czech weekly Reflex and founder of his own magazine, Raut . With Pavel Lev, he cofounded Studio Najbrt. For his film and theater posters, books, and other works, he received the Grand Prix at the 17th Biennial of Graphic Design in Brno in 1996, a Bronze Prize from the Tokyo Type Directors Club, five Czech Lion Awards, and the Czech Grand Design 2007 award. He designed Josef Koudelka: Next , a visual biography by Melissa Harris (2023), Invasion 68: Prague (2008), Theatre (2022), Returning (2018), Deníky (2021), the Czech edition of Diaries and several others.

article_text:
News

Gochman Collection of Indigenous Art to Open Katonah Space in November

The new home in New York, known as Branchline, will display selections from the family’s trove of over 800 contemporary Native artworks.

Branchline, a permanent exhibition space for the Gochman Family Collection, will open on November 6 in Katonah, New York, functioning as a new home for the renowned trove of contemporary Native art.

Building on the private collection's focus on Indigenous and anti-colonial art, Branchline will present rotating exhibitions of the over 800 works by contemporary Native artists in the Gochman Collection and provide residential and studio spaces for artists. Deriving its name from the network of rail lines that connect Katonah to surrounding areas like Manhattan and Upstate New York, Branchline also encompasses the ancestral and historical lineages informing the featured art.

"We imagine this as a flexible space to not only more broadly share the Collection, but to also create opportunities for varied audiences of artists, scholars, students, families, and our neighbors to spend time together," Laura Phipps, who became the collection's director in March , told Hyperallergic .

Designed by Elizabeth Roberts Architects and planted right next to the Katonah Metro-North station, the new site spans two historic buildings and a reconstructed barn. Open to the public four days a week and free of charge, Branchline's main gallery and annex will open next month, while its barn and sculpture deck will open in 2027. There are also two residential apartments above the main gallery for invited artists, and studio spaces to facilitate works in progress.

To set the tone for the site's communal vision, Branchline's inaugural exhibition, Line Break , curated by assistant curator Moonoka Begay (Ndee/Diné) with collection associate Nicole van Brugge, welcomes 18 artists from a range of practices and backgrounds. Intricate kené designs made by Sara Flores (Shipibo-Konibo), poetic paintings by Teresa Baker (Mandan/Hidatsa), and multimedia pieces by Jaune Quick-to-See Smith (an enrolled Salish member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Nation) are among the over two dozen works.

"As we considered how lines have been used to map land, chart time, and index lineage, we recognized a natural connection to the ongoing dialogues present in contemporary Indigenous art," Begay told Hyperallergic . " Line Break presents a selection of work that speaks to the many properties of lines and considers what happens when they divide, extend, bend, and even break."

When the Surface Thinks /

Oct 30 – Dec 18, 2026 / Opening: Thursday, Oct 29, 5pm – 8pm / Exhibition tour: Thursday, Oct 29, 5pm /

White Cube Hong Kong presents When the Surface Thinks , a solo exhibition by Paris-based Chinese artist Zhang Yunyao (b. 1985, Shanghai). With this new body of work, the artist contends that meaning can reside within a surface – proposing painting as a sentient field that registers, reflects and thinks.

The exhibition presents large-scale, illusionistic abstractions from Zhang’s ‘Connector’ series (2022–present), tight close-ups of carved heads from the ‘Time’ series (2021–present), and studies of classical statuary. These works subvert the traditions of Soviet Realism and the French Beaux-Arts that informed Zhang’s early academic training.

Central to the artist’s practice is his use of graphite on felt, a material that is both light-absorbent and resistant to revision. Unlike oil on canvas, which allows for overpainting and correction, graphite becomes embedded into the textured plane. Through a sustained and highly physical process, Zhang builds tonal depth across the textile’s flatness, creating images that appear at once sculptural and weightless.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 在首届Manufactory x ArtReview驻留作家项目中，汉娜·佩扎克（Hannah Pezzack）倾听了帕克罗亚尔隐秘的工业节奏以及处于重新开发中的风景

ArtReview驻留作家项目中，汉娜·佩扎克倾听了帕克罗亚尔隐秘的工业节奏以及处于重新开发中的风景。", "links": [{"text": "Manufactory x ArtReview Writer’s Residency", "url": "https://www.parkroyaldesigndistrict.com/prdd-programme/residencyartreview2026"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在一个闷热八月的午后，我发现自己正漫步在伦敦最大工业园区帕克罗亚尔（Park Royal）盘错的主干道与小巷间。自20世纪初以来，这里便是英国工业的腹地，曾孕育雷诺（Renault）、亨氏（Heinz）和健力士（Guinness）等家喻户晓的品牌，如今依然是生产与分销的重要枢纽。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这里，工业在卷帘门和装货湾后展开，伴随着货车与铰接式卡车源源不断地进出。面包、啤酒和饼干与切割石材、金属和专用机械一同涌现；托盘被装载，货物被发运，材料被运往他处。这是一个由集装箱、算法和制造厂交织而成的复杂网络，将大伦敦与更广阔的世界连接起来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着我向园区更深处走去，我遇到了从通风井中喷薄而出的蒸汽团，空气中弥漫着夏末的热气。当我穿行于狭窄的小巷时，衬衫紧紧贴在背上，偶能擦肩而过身穿高可见度夹克的工作人员。我随身携带一套现场录音设备——腰间挂着Zoom录音机，三脚架上装着麦克风，上面套着被称为“死猫”的毛茸茸灰色防风罩——这引来了一些好奇的目光或半含羞涩的微笑，但大多数时候我都被忽视了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_5915-1230x1640.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "图片由作者提供", "credit": "ArtReview", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在漫步途中，我注意到帕克罗亚尔有很大一部分隐匿于视线之外。它的建筑在很大程度上具有隐蔽性：隐现的战后建筑、没有窗户的单元以及预制棚屋几乎没有透露出内部正在发生什么的线索。然而，在这些冷峻的外表背后，却存在着多声部的活动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有些噪音溢出到街道上，肉耳已经可以听到，但通过我的耳机，这些声音变得宏大开阔，从背景的嗡嗡声中剥离出来，被清晰地带到前台。我停下脚步，将麦克风高高举向天空，倾听着切割花岗岩的刺耳声；倒车的叉车；在水泥地上拖拽的板条箱；某个隐蔽处传来的嘈杂收音机声；大声的指令；货车门的猛地关上声；半听真切的对话声与笑声。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，倾听成了一种无需侵入其运作就能理解这片隐蔽景观的方式。通过我的录音设备，我可以在某种程度上窥探仓库内部和拐角周围，一窥正在发生的事情。用理论家布兰登·拉贝尔（Brandon LaBelle）的话来说，声音是“滥交的”：它穿透墙壁和地板，跨越边界，携带着原本看不见或被隐形之物的痕迹。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但帕克罗亚尔与可视性之间令人不安的关系不仅限于其建筑。尽管园区内包含了如此多的活动——并且对伦敦的日常运作如此重要——但这片庞大的场地在很大程度上仍然缺席于城市的文化想象中。它的产品到处流通；而生产它们的那些过程和人员——通常拿着低薪、处于不稳定就业中——却大多隐匿不见。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通过这种方式，帕克罗亚尔可以被理解为一种腹地：那些难以定义的地理区域之一，包含农田、港口、码头和交通走廊——这些地区在维持交换系统的同时，在政治上仍然处于边缘。正如研究人员尼尔·布伦纳（Neil Brenner）和尼科斯·卡齐基斯（Nikos Katsikis）所观察到的那样，尽管腹地在支撑全球资本主义方面发挥着至关重要作用，但此类地带仍然“有点像一个‘黑匣子’”，经常被塑造成“未被绘制地图的、落后的、因而不值得了解的”区域。这种态度在该词的词源中得到了呼应：它源自德语Hinterland，字面意思是“背后的土地”，它唤起了一种从视线中退去、被忽视的地方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_5900-1230x1640.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "图片由作者提供", "credit": "ArtReview", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我所创作的音景由多层现场录音交织而成，它试图放大那些通常被推到边缘的运作，同时唤起人们对该地区复杂的声学特性的关注。帕克罗亚尔以其自身错综复杂的节奏和多元的声音而嗡嗡作响。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但这里捕捉到的声学生态同样也是脆弱的。由于被指定为工业用途（这限制了住宅开发），这片土地长期以来一直免受伦敦投机性房地产市场最糟糕冲击的影响。相对较低的租金反过来让一个意想不到的世界组合在传统工业旁扎根：小规模制造商与工匠；艺术家与电影制作人；为不同社群服务的咖啡馆、面包店、餐馆和水烟馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这一独特的生态系统现在正面临着模糊的前景。帕克罗亚尔坐落于城市重大变革的中心，HS2铁路线以及老橡树（Old Oak）周边的更广泛再开发项目将带来新的投资。随着地价上涨，人们担心可承受性会被侵蚀，这给小型企业和独立创作者带来了特别的压力，其中许多人本就因2019冠状病毒病（COVID-19）疫情而苦苦挣扎。因此，问题不仅在于帕克罗亚尔将变成什么样，而在于什么——以及谁——能够留下来。在这种语境下听来，这段录音不仅仅是一幅听觉肖像：它记录了一个地方，而其独特的共振可能很快就会发生面目全非的改变。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_5942-1230x1640.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "图片由作者提供", "credit": "ArtReview", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种迫在眉睫的失落感把我带回了南威尔士——我长大的后工业腹地，它与帕克皇家（Park Royal）的相似之处最初点燃了我对这个工业区的兴趣。小时候，我常和父亲一起去加的夫湾（Cardiff Bay），他在前码头区的熔炉里工作过。这里曾是重工业中心，到2000年代初，海滨已被改造为休闲区：那些熏黑的建筑、绞盘和码头被高耸的公寓和歌剧院构成的奢华建筑群所取代。父亲熟悉的大部分景物都已消失，但当我们在防波堤上漫步时，他会唤起人们对这里被遗忘的声音景观的记忆：穿过受污染港口的轮船、铁路车厢的隆隆声、炉火永不停歇的轰鸣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他的怀旧情绪是矛盾的。多年的体力劳动使他身体残疾，他对这份工作的肮脏、危险或无休止的噪声并没有多少好感。他怀念的是那些声音中恒常的稳定性，以及随之烟消云散的社会世界。散步时，他会指着那些不复存在的地点：他记得曾在那儿听过爵士乐和根源音乐的酒吧；被重新开发擦除或改造的街道；威尔士历史最悠久的多元族裔社区、流行、R&B和灵歌歌手雪莉·巴西（Shirley Bassey）的故乡——老虎湾（Tiger Bay）旧街区，该街区在1970年代大面积遭到拆除。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_5925-1230x1538.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtReview", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_5940-1230x1640.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "图片由作者提供", "credit": "ArtReview", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这一城市更新叙事中存在着一个重要的紧张关系。正因为其边缘性，腹地有时被称为“牺牲区”：其价值主要在于它们能向大都市提供什么，因此极易受到资源开采、忽视和彻底重塑之循环的侵害。加的夫码头蜕变为加的夫湾的过程，因其导致的士绅化效应以及未能造福历史上一直视该地区为家园的多元文化工人阶级社区而受到批评。这种流离失所的遗留问题，为帕克皇家的未来投下了令人不安的阴影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "带着这种不确定的前景，我在帕克皇家众多洗车场之一的外面结束了我的声音漫步，那里有一群工人正在用水管冲洗一辆银色掀背车布满灰尘的车前盖，并跟着一首嘻哈歌曲大声合唱。听着他们和谐的歌声，我笑了笑，选择不按下录音键，让这一刻完全属于他们。这也是该工业区声音生活的另一个令人惊奇的方面：由于几乎没有住宅邻居会抱怨噪声，该区域的声音领地从白天的作业一直延伸到深夜，工业的喧嚣让位于来自水烟馆和汽车音响里轰鸣出的音乐。至少在目前，帕克皇家依然喧闹、不羁且充满生机。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "汉娜·佩扎克（Hannah Pezzack）是一位常驻荷兰和英国的作家、编辑兼策展人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "讲座：2026年10月12日 Pezzack将与同为驻留作家的Aram Masharqa、Park I pause and raise my microphones skywards, listening to the screech of granite being sliced; a reversing forklift; crates dragged across concrete; a radio blaring somewhere out of sight; shouted instructions; the slam of a van door; a half-heard conversation, laughter."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Listening, then, becomes a way of apprehending this obscured landscape without intruding on its operations. Through my recording devices, I can, in a sense, peer into warehouses and around corners, catching a glimpse of the goings on. In the words of theorist Brandon LaBelle, sound is ‘promiscuous’: it travels through walls and floors, crosses boundaries, carrying traces of what otherwise goes unseen, or is made invisible."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But Park Royal’s uneasy relationship with visibility extends beyond its architecture. For all the action contained within the estate – and for all its importance to the everyday functioning of London – the vast site remains mostly absent from the city’s cultural imaginary. Its products circulate everywhere; the processes and people – often low-paid and in precarious employment – that produce them remain largely out of sight."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In this way, Park Royal can be understood as a hinterland: one of those difficult-to-define geographical areas that encompass farmland, ports, docklands and transport corridors – regions that sustain systems of exchange while remaining politically peripheral. As researchers Neil Brenner and Nikos Katsikis observe, despite the hinterland’s crucial role in supporting global capitalism, such zones remain ‘something of a “black box”’, frequently cast as ‘unmapped, backward, and therefore not worth knowing about.’ This attitude is echoed in the term’s etymology: derived from the German Hinterland , literally ‘the land behind’, it evokes a place that recedes from view, a place that is overlooked."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_5900-1230x1640.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Photo courtesy the author", "credit": "ArtReview"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The soundscape I have created, composed of layers of field recordings, is an attempt to amplify operations usually pushed to the margins, while drawing attention to the area’s complex sonic character. Park Royal thrums with its own intricate rhythms and manifold voices."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But the acoustic ecology captured here is also a fragile one. The land has long been insulated from the worst of London’s speculative property market by its designation for industrial use, which restricts residential development. Relatively low rents have, in turn, allowed an unlikely mixture of worlds to take root alongside the more conventional industries: small manufacturers and artisans; artists and filmmakers; cafés, bakeries, restaurants and shisha bars serving its diverse communities."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This particular ecosystem now faces an unclear horizon. Park Royal sits at the centre of significant urban change, with the HS2 railway line and wider redevelopment around Old Oak set to bring new investment. As land values rise, there are fears that the affordability will be eroded, placing particular pressure on smaller businesses and independent makers, many of whom were already strained by the COVID-19 pandemic. The question, then, is not simply what Park Royal will become, but what – and who – will be able to remain. Heard in this context, the recording is more than an auditory portrait: it is a record of a place whose particular resonances may soon be altered beyond recognition."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_5942-1230x1640.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Photo courtesy the author", "credit": "ArtReview"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The sense of impending loss brings me back to South Wales, the post-industrial hinterland where I grew up, whose parallels with Park Royal first sparked my interest in the estate. As a child, I would visit Cardiff Bay with my father, who had been employed in the furnaces of the former docklands. Once a centre of heavy industry, by the early 2000s the waterfront was being remade as a leisure district: its blackened buildings, winches and wharves replaced by an ostentatious outcrop of high-rise apartments and an opera house. Most of what my father had known had disappeared, but as we meandered along the pier he would conjure its forgotten soundscape: ships crossing the polluted harbour; the trundle of railway carriages; the ceaseless roar of the fires."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "His nostalgia was ambivalent. Years of manual labour had left him physically disabled, and he had little affection for the dirt, danger or relentless noise of the job. What he mourned was the measured of stability of those sounds, and the social world that had evaporated alongside it. As we walked, he would point to places that no longer existed: pubs where he remembered hearing jazz and roots music; streets erased or transformed by redevelopment; the old neighbourhood of Tiger Bay, Wales’s oldest multi-ethnic community and the birthplace of pop, R&B and soul singer Shirley Bassey, which was largely demolished in the 1970s."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_5925-1230x1538.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ArtReview"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_5940-1230x1640.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Photos courtesy the author", "credit": "ArtReview"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There is an important tension within this narrative of regeneration. Precisely because of their marginality, hinterlands are sometimes described as ‘sacrifice zones’: valued principally for what they can provide to the metropolis, and therefore vulnerable to cycles of extraction, neglect and sweeping reinvention. Cardiff Docks’ metamorphosis into Cardiff Bay has been criticised for its gentrifying effects, and for failing to benefit the multicultural, working-class communities that have historically called the area home. It is a legacy of displacement that casts an uneasy shadow over Park Royal’s future."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "With this uncertain prospect in mind, I conclude my soundwalk outside one of Park Royal’s many car washes, where a group of workers are hosing down the dusty bonnet of a silver hatchback, singing loudly along to a hip-hop track. I laugh as they harmonise, choosing not to hit record and allowing the moment to remain theirs. This is yet another surprising facet of the estate’s sonic life: with few residential neighbours to complain about the noise, the area’s acoustic territory extends beyond the working day and well into the night, the industrial clamour giving way to music from shisha bars and blasted out of car stereos. For now, at least, Park Royal remains noisy, unruly and very much alive."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Hannah Pezzack is a writer, editor and curator based in the Netherlands and the UK."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Talk : 12 October 2026 Pezzack will be in conversation with fellow writer-in-residence Aram Masharqa, programme director of Park Royal Design District Mazzy-Mae Green and ArtReview ’s Fi Churchman. article_text:
Audio produced by Hannah Pezzack, with mixing and mastering by Brandon Michael.

For the inaugural Manufactory x ArtReview Writer’s Residency , Hannah Pezzack listens to Park Royal’s hidden industrial rhythms and to a landscape in redevelopment.

On a humid afternoon in August, I find myself wandering the winding arterial roads and alleyways of Park Royal, London’s largest industrial estate. An epicentre of British industry since the early twentieth century, the area has been home to household names including Renault, Heinz and Guinness, and remains a major hub of production and distribution today.

Here, industry unfolds behind roller shutters and loading bays, in the constant coming and going of vans and articulated lorries. Bread, beer and biscuits emerge alongside cut stone, metal and specialist machinery; pallets are loaded, goods dispatched, materials carried elsewhere. It is an intricate latticework of containers, algorithms and manufacturing plants connecting Greater London to the wider world.

Journeying deeper into the estate, I encounter clouds of steam escaping from ventilation shafts, the air thick with the heat of late summer. My shirt sticks to my back as I slip down narrow lanes, passing the occasional worker in a high-vis jacket. Carrying a field-recording setup – a Zoom recorder attached to my belt and tripod-mounted microphones, replete with furry grey windshields known as ‘dead cats’ – I attract the odd curious glance or half-smile, but mostly I am ignored.

Along my walk, I note how much of Park Royal withholds itself from view. Its architecture is largely one of concealment: looming post-war buildings, windowless units and prefabricated sheds offer few clues as to what takes place within. Yet behind these stark exteriors lies a polyphony of activity.

Some of the noise spills out onto the street and is already audible to the naked ear, but through my headphones the sounds become expansive, detached from the background hum and brought sharply to the fore. I pause and raise my microphones skywards, listening to the screech of granite being sliced; a reversing forklift; crates dragged across concrete; a radio blaring somewhere out of sight; shouted instructions; the slam of a van door; a half-heard conversation, laughter.

Listening, then, becomes a way of apprehending this obscured landscape without intruding on its operations. Through my recording devices, I can, in a sense, peer into warehouses and around corners, catching a glimpse of the goings on. In the words of theorist Brandon LaBelle, sound is ‘promiscuous’: it travels through walls and floors, crosses boundaries, carrying traces of what otherwise goes unseen, or is made invisible.

But Park Royal’s uneasy relationship with visibility extends beyond its architecture. For all the action contained within the estate – and for all its importance to the everyday functioning of London – the vast site remains mostly absent from the city’s cultural imaginary. Its products circulate everywhere; the processes and people – often low-paid and in precarious employment – that produce them remain largely out of sight.

In this way, Park Royal can be understood as a hinterland: one of those difficult-to-define geographical areas that encompass farmland, ports, docklands and transport corridors – regions that sustain systems of exchange while remaining politically peripheral. As researchers Neil Brenner and Nikos Katsikis observe, despite the hinterland’s crucial role in supporting global capitalism, such zones remain ‘something of a “black box”’, frequently cast as ‘unmapped, backward, and therefore not worth knowing about.’ This attitude is echoed in the term’s etymology: derived from the German Hinterland , literally ‘the land behind’, it evokes a place that recedes from view, a place that is overlooked.

The soundscape I have created, composed of layers of field recordings, is an attempt to amplify operations usually pushed to the margins, while drawing attention to the area’s complex sonic character. Park Royal thrums with its own intricate rhythms and manifold voices.

But the acoustic ecology captured here is also a fragile one. The land has long been insulated from the worst of London’s speculative property market by its designation for industrial use, which restricts residential development. Relatively low rents have, in turn, allowed an unlikely mixture of worlds to take root alongside the more conventional industries: small manufacturers and artisans; artists and filmmakers; cafés, bakeries, restaurants and shisha bars serving its diverse communities.

This particular ecosystem now faces an unclear horizon. Park Royal sits at the centre of significant urban change, with the HS2 railway line and wider redevelopment around Old Oak set to bring new investment. As land values rise, there are fears that the affordability will be eroded, placing particular pressure on smaller businesses and independent makers, many of whom were already strained by the COVID-19 pandemic. The question, then, is not simply what Park Royal will become, but what – and who – will be able to remain. Heard in this context, the recording is more than an auditory portrait: it is a record of a place whose particular resonances may soon be altered beyond recognition.

The sense of impending loss brings me back to South Wales, the post-industrial hinterland where I grew up, whose parallels with Park Royal first sparked my interest in the estate. As a child, I would visit Cardiff Bay with my father, who had been employed in the furnaces of the former docklands. Once a centre of heavy industry, by the early 2000s the waterfront was being remade as a leisure district: its blackened buildings, winches and wharves replaced by an ostentatious outcrop of high-rise apartments and an opera house. Most of what my father had known had disappeared, but as we meandered along the pier he would conjure its forgotten soundscape: ships crossing the polluted harbour; the trundle of railway carriages; the ceaseless roar of the fires.

His nostalgia was ambivalent. Years of manual labour had left him physically disabled, and he had little affection for the dirt, danger or relentless noise of the job. What he mourned was the measured of stability of those sounds, and the social world that had evaporated alongside it. As we walked, he would point to places that no longer existed: pubs where he remembered hearing jazz and roots music; streets erased or transformed by redevelopment; the old neighbourhood of Tiger Bay, Wales’s oldest multi-ethnic community and the birthplace of pop, R&B and soul singer Shirley Bassey, which was largely demolished in the 1970s.

There is an important tension within this narrative of regeneration. Precisely because of their marginality, hinterlands are sometimes described as ‘sacrifice zones’: valued principally for what they can provide to the metropolis, and therefore vulnerable to cycles of extraction, neglect and sweeping reinvention. Cardiff Docks’ metamorphosis into Cardiff Bay has been criticised for its gentrifying effects, and for failing to benefit the multicultural, working-class communities that have historically called the area home. It is a legacy of displacement that casts an uneasy shadow over Park Royal’s future.

With this uncertain prospect in mind, I conclude my soundwalk outside one of Park Royal’s many car washes, where a group of workers are hosing down the dusty bonnet of a silver hatchback, singing loudly along to a hip-hop track. I laugh as they harmonise, choosing not to hit record and allowing the moment to remain theirs. This is yet another surprising facet of the estate’s sonic life: with few residential neighbours to complain about the noise, the area’s acoustic territory extends beyond the working day and well into the night, the industrial clamour giving way to music from shisha bars and blasted out of car stereos. For now, at least, Park Royal remains noisy, unruly and very much alive.

Hannah Pezzack is a writer, editor and curator based in the Netherlands and the UK.

article_text:
Two films have won five of the prizes at the Busan Asian Project Market (APM).

Indonesian director Aditya Ahmad’s “ Goldfish ” took three and Indian filmmaker Tribeny Rai’s “ A Chronicle of Minor Things ” (working title) took two. The awards were part of the Asian Contents & Film Market’s (ACFM) first combined ceremony.

“Goldfish” won the QCinema Special Award, the Kongchak Studio Award and the VIPO Award. Ahmad’s first feature is set in South Sulawesi, where he grew up, and centers on a boy who flees his father. Muhammad Zaidy and Meiske Taurisia are producing. The project also received money from this year’s ACF Script Development Fund. It was selected for APM, where it took part in business meetings.

Related Stories

'SNL U.K.' Cold Open Sees Reunion Between Prince William and Kate and Prince Harry and Meghan (With Some Help From Former Prince Andrew): 'They Must Want Us to Be Royals Again!'

Peacock App Launches 'Your Bravoverse,' Featuring a Personalized TikTok-Style Video Feed Hosted by AI-Generated Andy Cohen

Rai’s project is produced by Kislay and took the Sørfond Award and the APM Busan Award. The APM Busan Award recognized its original story and structure, and the way Rai works a social issue quietly into the narrative. The citation also said its setting and themes could appeal to audiences outside India.

Six other projects also won APM awards. Actor-director Reza Rahadian’s “Casparina” is a family drama built from a personal story. It won the CJ ENM Award. Kim Jinyeong’s “Red Hunger” won the Kantana Picture Award, and Panu Aree’s “Fātimah” won the Kantana Virtual Production Award. Yen Hao-hsuan’s “Uncle” draws on the director’s own life to look at family, shame and belonging as Taiwan changes fast. It took the CathayPlay Award and was praised for giving a character with an intellectual disability full depth and dignity. Park Syeyoung’s “Satellite of Love” won the Songwon Award, and E Del Mundo’s “Once Upon a Time in the Philippines” won the ArteKino International Award.

APM’s submissions hit a record 604 this year, from 48 countries. Its official selection had 30 projects from 17 countries, and eight of them shared prizes across 11 categories.

“Today’s awards recognize the promise of these projects and the stories they have yet to bring to life. ACFM’s awards do not end in Busan. They travel on to Jakarta, Manila, Oslo and Bangkok,” said ACFM director Ellen Y.D. Kim.

At the ceremony, ACFM also honored three international co-productions with Korean involvement that won the ACF Co-Production Support Fund in August. Fukada Koji’s “Grateful” gets KRW60 million ($41,700). Jakrawal Nilthamrong’s “Rhizome” and Boo Junfeng’s “Trinity” get KRW40 million ($27,800) each.

Doc Square gave out two new prizes at its documentary work-in-progress showcase. Three projects won the Impact Asia Award, and each receives $5,000. They were Ma Chi Hang’s “Moon Is Watching You,” Jang Minkyung’s “Our Waves,” and “Restless Farewell,” directed by Yang Nan and He Peiyun. “Restless Farewell” is about young migrant workers in precarious jobs in Shanghai, and it also won the Newstapa Award. That prize includes KRW10 million ($6,900) for production. Once the film is complete, it will also have the chance to screen a 60-minute cut on the Newstapa Foundation’s channels.

From the Busan Story Market, “My Upstairs Neighbors” from Clayhouse and “Friend Request” from Ryoung Studio won the JAFF Market IP Connection Award. Both will go to Indonesia’s Jogja-NETPAC Asian Film Festival for its JAFF IP Connection program. At InnoAsia, Taiwan’s imCore Corp. won the MPS Award, chosen by industry votes. Korean startups Lumicraft and Reproduction took the AWS Award, which comes with KRW10 million ($6,900) in AWS cloud vouchers. Lumicraft makes an AI casting platform called Castlink. Reproduction makes Pre-Flow, a tool for screenplay analysis and sharing production data.

APM hosted 746 business meetings with 133 companies. The Busan Story Market held 520 meetings with 136 companies. ACFM ran Oct. 10–13, and the Busan International Film Festival continues through Oct. 15.

title_original: Close to the Free World
editorial_title_zh: 接近自由的世界
editorial_excerpt_zh: 监狱电影：菲利普·范斯·史密斯二世反思《人生》《监狱》和《辛辛那提》等电影如何描绘监狱生活，以及他多年来观看这些电影的经历如何改变
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "当北卡罗来纳州中央监狱在2004年向囚犯放映喜剧片《人生》（1999）时，我无法坚持看完30分钟。这部电影由艾迪·墨菲和马丁·劳伦斯主演，讲述的是两位来自纽约的私酒贩子被错误地判谋杀罪，被送往1930年代密西西比州的终身监禁。我的朋友们笑得喘不过气来。但25岁的我，已经因为谋杀罪被判无期徒刑，服刑两年了。在屏幕上看到无数被关押的黑人男子——就像我一样——并不觉得有趣，不管我多么喜欢看电影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "每周五的电影之夜让我尽可能接近自由世界。我和朋友们带着薯片、苏打水和一品脱冰淇淋走进拥挤的礼堂。在120分钟里，我逃离了监狱，惊叹于间谍揭露世界统治的邪恶阴谋，弱者克服卑微出身取得伟大成就，以及我永远无法亲自看到的异国风光。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但作为一名囚犯观看关于监狱的电影摧毁了我对逃避现实的幻想。我不喜欢这些电影如何依赖囚犯的刻板印象来推动故事。它们往往将暴力视为男性表达脆弱而非刚强的必然结果。它们强化了社会对普通囚犯的刻板印象，即一个无法被改造的极端男性化恶棍。在这些电影——如《橄榄球帮》（2006）、《无冕之王》（2002）和《最长的跑道》（2005）——中，黑人囚犯与昔日的黑脸秀中快乐的奴隶并无二致。我看到的角色并没有描绘我的现实，所以我摒弃了它们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管我对监狱电影有所顾虑，但我理解好莱坞的动机。将一名被定罪的杀人犯描绘成英雄是具有挑战性的。生锈的匕首永远不会比圣剑更耀眼。因此，监狱电影中的英雄通常是无辜的，对白人观众来说是容易产生共鸣的，这与真正填满美国监狱的人群大相径庭。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在我入狱之前，我并不总是讨厌关于监狱的电影。我青少年时期喜欢了不少这类电影。《坏男孩》（1983）是我记得最喜欢的第一部监狱题材电影。在这部电影中，16岁的米克·奥布莱恩（肖恩·潘饰）在一次毒品交易失败导致一名8岁男孩死亡的车祸中被送进了野蛮的青少年监狱。男孩的哥哥帕科·莫雷诺（埃萨伊·莫拉莱斯饰）为了能被送进同一个监狱以报复被杀的弟弟，袭击了米克的女友。米克被迫为生存而战（在一幕中，他用装满未开封汽水罐的枕套作为自卫武器），成为了一个可以被救赎的角色。我欣赏《坏男孩》因为它描绘了一个弱者战胜敌人的情节，但当时我没有注意到其中的隐含意义：一个罪犯只有在是一个叛逆的白人青少年时，才能成为一个可以被理解、讨人喜欢的角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我青少年时期在父亲的盗版VHS录像带中发现了20世纪70年代的黑人剥削电影《惩教所》（1979），这些电影呈现了一种不同的罪犯——以及一种不同的共鸣。这部电影的主角“太甜”（莱昂·艾萨克·肯尼迪饰）被不公正地送进了监狱，作为他的第一次考验，他必须抵御臭名昭著的监狱掠食者“半死”（巴贾·多拉饰）。当电影中那些留着非洲发型的灵魂兄弟们设法欺骗种族主义的白人中尉时，我笑了，但那时的我太天真，无法理解这部电影的真正含义。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“太甜”代表了20世纪60年代和70年代初出现的“黑人强硬派”形象，当时黑人美国人正在种族隔离制度结束后重新定义自己的身份。那时，美国利用监禁来压制黑人活动家，比如黑豹党的成员。作为回应，这些活动家从加利福尼亚州的索莱达监狱到纽约州的阿提卡监狱，甚至北卡罗来纳州的中央监狱，引发了监狱暴动。狱中的团结进一步推动了社会革命。《惩教所》体现了新发现的黑人勇敢精神，正如那个时代的其他反主流文化黑人电影一样，比如《超级飞侠》（1972）和《黑帮老大》（1973），只要黑人角色足够强硬以战胜种族主义当局，就连皮条客也可以成为主角。这些电影为现代电影如《说唱人生》（2005）铺平了道路，该片由特伦斯·霍华德主演。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一些电影将监狱描绘为英雄必须经历的成人礼，以实现个人成长。要征服监狱，英雄会遇到一位智者导师。在《马尔科姆·X》（1992）中，马尔科姆·小（丹泽尔·华盛顿饰）遇到被监禁的穆斯林，他们帮助他戒毒并找到作为领导者的自我声音。在《南中央》（1992）中，鲍比·约翰逊（格伦·普拉默饰）遇到一位父亲般的角色，帮助他获得假释，以便他能出去抚养年幼的儿子。监狱电影中的导师们引导迷失的灵魂从自我毁灭的道路上走向正途，这正是我在自己生活中经历过的。作为一名24岁的终身监禁者，我遇到了一位名叫鲍比·辛克莱尔的黑人退伍军人，他自1977年以来一直在服终身监禁，因谋杀罪而入狱。他在中央监狱秘密教我功夫，以免我加入帮派。除了教我影子踢和撞击拳，辛克莱尔还教我如何与其它囚犯打交道，帮助我处理监狱中的复杂情况。如果没有他的指导，我可能会加入帮派，使我的生活陷入混乱而非成就。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在《Sing Sing》（2023）中，科曼·多明戈饰演约翰·“神圣G”·惠特菲尔德，一名因未犯的罪行而服刑数十年的囚犯剧作家。神圣G不断遭遇假释被拒和好友迈克·迈克（塞恩·桑·何塞饰）的意外死亡，但他仍通过一个允许囚犯在监狱内上演戏剧的项目，指导并重塑了名叫克拉伦斯·“神圣眼”·马克林（以他本人为原型的戏剧化版本）的恶棍的人生。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与神圣G不同，我并不是一个无辜的人，因此无法认同他洗清冤屈的挣扎。2002年，北卡罗来纳州的一个陪审团裁定我犯有杀人罪，当时我试图抢劫一名男子进行毒品交易。我需要钱，因为我刚从因小罪入狱一年后被释放，当时无家可归。为了阻止抢劫，他掏出一把黑色塑料手枪，我误以为是致命武器。当我开枪时，我认为自己是在自卫。但法院的判决不同。自入狱以来，我发表了大量作品，追求高等教育，并在写作工作坊中教我的同监犯，但我仍然在监狱中——在服刑23年后——没有任何释放的希望。更糟糕的是，我必须忍受杀害了一个本不可能伤害我的人的悔恨。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我糟糕的人生轨迹永远不会成为一部电影的灵感。但《Sing Sing》反映了我的悲伤，我放弃希望的诱惑，以及我害怕死在牢笼中的恐惧。作为一名作家，我最能理解的是Divine G如何依赖艺术作为支撑。我无法将他视为电影中的一个角色。Divine G代表了我曾经一起服刑的每一个男人。当他在电影中强大到无法为自己哭泣时，我为他哭泣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Sing Sing》给了我勇气，在最近一次有线电视重播《Life》时看完它，这距离我当初中途离场已经过去了20多年。这次，伯尼·麦克让我笑得肚子疼。尽管这部电影讽刺了监禁的艰辛，但我认出了其中贯穿始终的韧性主题。主角雷和克劳德即使在牢狱之灾半个世纪后，也从未停止寻求自由。当生活看似毫无希望时，他们通过希望度过三次冲突。从那以后，我停止将监狱电影视为娱乐来源，现在我将其视为灵感的宝库。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "When North Carolina’s Central Prison showed the buddy comedy Life (1999) to the incarcerated population in 2004, I couldn’t sit through more than 30 minutes. The film, starring Eddie Murphy and Martin Lawrence, follows a pair of bootleggers from New York who are wrongly convicted of murder and sent to prison for life in 1930s Mississippi. My friends laughed until they lost their breath. But at 25 years old, I had already served two years on a life-without-parole sentence for murder. Watching a multitude of caged Black men—like me—on screen didn’t seem entertaining, no matter how much I loved going to the movies."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Movie night on Fridays at Central Prison brought me as close to the free world as I could get. My friends and I brought chips, sodas, and pints of ice cream to the packed auditorium. For 120 minutes, I escaped prison to marvel at spies uncovering diabolical plots for world domination, underdogs overcoming humble origins to achieve great things, and visuals of exotic locales that I will never see in person while serving life."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But watching films about prison while incarcerated destroyed my idea of escapism. I didn’t like how these films relied on stereotypes about prisoners to carry a story. Often, they portray violence as the accepted consequence for men who express vulnerability instead of toughness. They reinforce society’s image of the common prisoner as a hypermasculine thug who could never rehabilitate. In these movies—like Gridiron Gang (2006), Undisputed (2002), and The Longest Yard (2005)—Black prisoners are no better than happy slaves in minstrel shows of yesteryear. The characters I saw didn’t depict my reality, so I shunned them."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Despite my concerns about prison movies, I understand the Hollywood motive. Portraying a convicted killer as a hero is challenging. A rusty shank will never gleam brighter than Excalibur. So heroes in prison films are usually innocent and relatable to a Caucasian audience, which is a far cry from who really fills American prisons."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I didn’t always dislike films about prison. Before my incarceration, I enjoyed quite a few. Bad Boys (1983) was the first prison film I remember liking as a teen. In it, 16-year-old Mick O’Brien (Sean Penn) is sent to a wild youth prison after he crashes a stolen car during a drug deal gone wrong, killing an 8-year-old boy. The boy’s older brother, Paco Moreno (Esai Morales), assaults Mick’s girlfriend in a bid to be sent to the same prison, so he can avenge his slain sibling. Mick, forced to fight for his life (wielding, in one scene, a pillowcase stuffed with unopened soda cans for self-defense), becomes a redeemable character. I appreciated Bad Boys because it depicted an underdog besting his enemies, but back then I didn’t pick up on the subtext: that a criminal can be a relatable, likable character only if he’s a rebellious white teen."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The 1970s Blaxploitation films like Penitentiary (1979), which I found in my father’s pirated VHS collection as a teenager, presented a different kind of criminal—and a different kind of relatability. The film’s hero, Too Sweet (Leon Isaac Kennedy), lands in prison unjustly, and as his first test, must fend off the notorious prison predator Half Dead (Badja Djola). I giggled when the Afroed soul brothers in the film schemed to hoodwink the racist white lieutenant, but I was too naïve, then, to understand the film’s true message."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Too Sweet represented the emerging “Black tough” of the 1960s and ’70s, when Black Americans were redefining their identity after the end of segregation. Back then, America weaponized incarceration to silence Black activists, like members of the Black Panther Party. In response, these activists instigated prison riots from Soledad in California to Attica in New York, and even Central Prison in North Carolina. Solidarity behind bars furthered the social revolution. Penitentiary embodied a newly discovered Black bravado, as did other countercultural Black films of that time, like Super Fly (1972) and The Mack (1973), in which even pimps could be protagonists as long as they were tough enough to trump the racist authorities. Those films paved the way for modern films like Hustle & Flow (2005), starring Terrence Howard."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Some movies incorporate prison as a rite of passage a hero must endure for personal growth. To conquer prison, the hero meets a wise mentor. In Malcolm X (1992), Malcolm Little (Denzel Washington) encounters incarcerated Muslims who help him kick dope and find his voice as a leader. In South Central (1992), Bobby Johnson (Glenn Plummer) meets a father figure who helps him earn parole so he can get out to raise his young son. Mentors in prison films guide broken souls from a path of self-destruction to one of righteousness, something I experienced in my own life. As a 24-year-old lifer, I met a man I’ll call Bobby Sinclair, a Black Army veteran who had been serving life for murder since 1977. He taught me kung fu in secret at Central Prison so that I wouldn’t join a gang. Along with showing me shadow kicks and battering-ram punches, Sinclair helped me navigate prison by teaching me the intricacies of dealing with other convicts. Without his mentorship, I probably would’ve joined a gang, making my life one of turmoil instead of accomplishment."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Sing Sing (2023), Colman Domingo plays John “Divine G” Whitfield, an incarcerated playwright serving decades for a crime he didn’t commit. Divine G struggles with repeated denials of parole and the unexpected death of his friend Mike Mike (Sean San José), but somehow, he mentors and reshapes the life of a thug named Clarence “Divine Eye” Maclin (cast as a dramatized version of himself) through a program that enables incarcerated folks to put on plays in prison."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Unlike Divine G, I am not an innocent man, so I can’t identify with his struggle to clear his name. In 2002, a North Carolina jury convicted me of killing a man after trying to rob him during a drug deal. article_text:
When North Carolina’s Central Prison showed the buddy comedy Life (1999) to the incarcerated population in 2004, I couldn’t sit through more than 30 minutes. The film, starring Eddie Murphy and Martin Lawrence, follows a pair of bootleggers from New York who are wrongly convicted of murder and sent to prison for life in 1930s Mississippi. My friends laughed until they lost their breath. But at 25 years old, I had already served two years on a life-without-parole sentence for murder. Watching a multitude of caged Black men—like me—on screen didn’t seem entertaining, no matter how much I loved going to the movies.

Movie night on Fridays at Central Prison brought me as close to the free world as I could get. My friends and I brought chips, sodas, and pints of ice cream to the packed auditorium. For 120 minutes, I escaped prison to marvel at spies uncovering diabolical plots for world domination, underdogs overcoming humble origins to achieve great things, and visuals of exotic locales that I will never see in person while serving life.

But watching films about prison while incarcerated destroyed my idea of escapism. I didn’t like how these films relied on stereotypes about prisoners to carry a story. Often, they portray violence as the accepted consequence for men who express vulnerability instead of toughness. They reinforce society’s image of the common prisoner as a hypermasculine thug who could never rehabilitate. In these movies—like Gridiron Gang (2006), Undisputed (2002), and The Longest Yard (2005)—Black prisoners are no better than happy slaves in minstrel shows of yesteryear. The characters I saw didn’t depict my reality, so I shunned them.

Despite my concerns about prison movies, I understand the Hollywood motive. Portraying a convicted killer as a hero is challenging. A rusty shank will never gleam brighter than Excalibur. So heroes in prison films are usually innocent and relatable to a Caucasian audience, which is a far cry from who really fills American prisons.

I didn’t always dislike films about prison. Before my incarceration, I enjoyed quite a few. Bad Boys (1983) was the first prison film I remember liking as a teen. In it, 16-year-old Mick O’Brien (Sean Penn) is sent to a wild youth prison after he crashes a stolen car during a drug deal gone wrong, killing an 8-year-old boy. The boy’s older brother, Paco Moreno (Esai Morales), assaults Mick’s girlfriend in a bid to be sent to the same prison, so he can avenge his slain sibling. Mick, forced to fight for his life (wielding, in one scene, a pillowcase stuffed with unopened soda cans for self-defense), becomes a redeemable character. I appreciated Bad Boys because it depicted an underdog besting his enemies, but back then I didn’t pick up on the subtext: that a criminal can be a relatable, likable character only if he’s a rebellious white teen.

The 1970s Blaxploitation films like Penitentiary (1979), which I found in my father’s pirated VHS collection as a teenager, presented a different kind of criminal—and a different kind of relatability. The film’s hero, Too Sweet (Leon Isaac Kennedy), lands in prison unjustly, and as his first test, must fend off the notorious prison predator Half Dead (Badja Djola). I giggled when the Afroed soul brothers in the film schemed to hoodwink the racist white lieutenant, but I was too naïve, then, to understand the film’s true message.

Too Sweet represented the emerging “Black tough” of the 1960s and ’70s, when Black Americans were redefining their identity after the end of segregation. Back then, America weaponized incarceration to silence Black activists, like members of the Black Panther Party. In response, these activists instigated prison riots from Soledad in California to Attica in New York, and even Central Prison in North Carolina. Solidarity behind bars furthered the social revolution. Penitentiary embodied a newly discovered Black bravado, as did other countercultural Black films of that time, like Super Fly (1972) and The Mack (1973), in which even pimps could be protagonists as long as they were tough enough to trump the racist authorities. Those films paved the way for modern films like Hustle & Flow (2005), starring Terrence Howard.

Some movies incorporate prison as a rite of passage a hero must endure for personal growth. To conquer prison, the hero meets a wise mentor. In Malcolm X (1992), Malcolm Little (Denzel Washington) encounters incarcerated Muslims who help him kick dope and find his voice as a leader. In South Central (1992), Bobby Johnson (Glenn Plummer) meets a father figure who helps him earn parole so he can get out to raise his young son. Mentors in prison films guide broken souls from a path of self-destruction to one of righteousness, something I experienced in my own life. As a 24-year-old lifer, I met a man I’ll call Bobby Sinclair, a Black Army veteran who had been serving life for murder since 1977. He taught me kung fu in secret at Central Prison so that I wouldn’t join a gang. Along with showing me shadow kicks and battering-ram punches, Sinclair helped me navigate prison by teaching me the intricacies of dealing with other convicts. Without his mentorship, I probably would’ve joined a gang, making my life one of turmoil instead of accomplishment.

In Sing Sing (2023), Colman Domingo plays John “Divine G” Whitfield, an incarcerated playwright serving decades for a crime he didn’t commit. Divine G struggles with repeated denials of parole and the unexpected death of his friend Mike Mike (Sean San José), but somehow, he mentors and reshapes the life of a thug named Clarence “Divine Eye” Maclin (cast as a dramatized version of himself) through a program that enables incarcerated folks to put on plays in prison.

Unlike Divine G, I am not an innocent man, so I can’t identify with his struggle to clear his name. In 2002, a North Carolina jury convicted me of killing a man after trying to rob him during a drug deal. I needed cash because I had recently been released from a year in prison for petty crimes, and was then homeless. To thwart the robbery, he pulled out a black plastic pistol that I mistook as a deadly firearm. When I fired my gun, I thought I was protecting myself. The courts ruled differently. Since being incarcerated, I have published a plethora of writings, pursued higher education, and taught my peers in a writing workshop, but I remain in prison—after 23 years—with no hope for release. Worse, I live with the regret of having killed someone who couldn’t have hurt me.

My horrid character arc will never inspire a feature film. But Sing Sing reflects my grief, my temptation to give up hope, and my fear of dying in a cage. As a writer, I relate most to how Divine G leans on his art as a crutch. I couldn’t view him as a character in a film. Divine G represented every man I pulled time with. And when he was too strong to cry for himself in the film, I cried for him.

Sing Sing gave me the courage to finish watching Life when it aired on cable TV recently, more than 20 years after I walked out on it. This time, Bernie Mac made me laugh until my stomach hurt. Even though the film parodies the hardships of incarceration, I recognized an overarching theme of resilience. The main characters, Ray and Claude, never stop seeking freedom, even after a half century behind bars. They survive three acts of conflict by hoping when life seems hopeless. Ever since then, I’ve stopped viewing prison films as a source of entertainment, and now I embrace them as a wealth of inspiration.

article_text:
Jennifer Lawrence revealed on the “Call Her Daddy” podcast that she once discovered while filming a nude scene that there were crew members on set who were not approved to be there during the filming of such intimate material. The incident prompted Lawrence to “come down hard” on the crew and remains one of the definitive moments in her acting career that taught her the importance of speaking out.

When asked if she’s gotten more comfortable over the years in advocating for herself, Lawrence responded: “You have to be malleable. That’s part of the job. When Lynne Ramsay for ‘Die My Love’ says cut your hair and get mullet bangs and dye it platinum blonde… that’s the gig. You have to be malleable. But I definitely speak up more now because I am aware of the place I have in the industry.”

“There was an instance on set where crew members who were not approved when I was doing nudity were on set. I came down hard on it, purely because if we are not setting that principle then what on earth is going to happen to an 18-year-old unknown when she shows up and there’s people on set who are not approved to be there? She’s going to be in a position of do I say something and get a reputation for being difficult or do I let these people who I’m not comfortable with see me naked. It was important to me to explain that to the people why that was not okay.”

Lawrence is no stranger to nudity or sex scenes in her movie. She went viral last year for her comments about forgoing an intimacy coordinator during the filming of “Die My Love” with Robert Pattinson.

“We did not have [an intimacy coordinator], or maybe we did but we didn’t really… I felt really safe with Rob,” Lawrence said on the “Las Culturistas podcast. “He is not pervy and very in love with [partner] Suki Waterhouse. We mostly were just talking about our kids and relationships. There was never any weird like, ‘Does he think I like him?’ If there was a little bit of that I would probably have an intimacy coordinator. A lot of male actors get offended if you don’t want to fuck them, and then the punishment starts. He was not like that.”

As for the movie’s nude scenes: “I don’t care about nudity. I’m not sensitive about it. I wanted Lynne to have total freedom artistically… I think being pregnant took a lot of, like, vanity anxiety away. Before ‘No Hard Feelings,’ I was dieting and not eating carbs and working out. I was pregnant [for ‘Die My Love’]. Like, what was I gonna do? Not eat? I was working 15 hours a day. I was just tired… I remember, like, them sending over a close-up of cellulite and being like, ‘Do you want us to touch this up?’ And I was like, ‘No. That’s an ass.’”

Watch Lawrence’s full interview on “Call Her Daddy” in the video below.

article_text:
Art Movements

Danh Vo and Sandra Mujinga Selected for Met Museum Commissions

Genesis Facade and Great Hall artists announced, a new leader for the Armenian Museum of America, Bernie Sanders weighs in on the AI art debate, and more.

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

The Met's 2027 Genesis Facade and Great Hall Commissions

Artist Danh Vo was chosen for the Metropolitan Museum of Art's 2027 Genesis Facade commission, and Sandra Mujinga was selected for the Great Hall commission. Vo, who often entwines his experience as a Vietnamese boat refugee with questionings of modern history, will create new works for the four niches of the museum's Beaux-Arts exterior, on view starting in September. Mujinga, whose practice draws from the legacy of Afrofuturism, science fiction, and post-colonialism, will present a site-specific installation in the institution's interior next November.

“Danh Vo and Sandra Mujinga both treat history as something alive and unsettled and are deeply attuned to the ways objects and bodies carry meaning across time," Met Director and CEO Max Hollein said in a statement.

Sarah Hayes Named Deputy Director of Armenian Museum

Sarah Hayes , who had led the Armenian Museum of America's (AMoA) Development department since 2023, has been named deputy director of the Massachusetts institution. Her immersion in Armenian culture, history, and human rights goes back decades, when she served as a Peace Corps Volunteer in the nation from 2005 to 2007. Hayes later worked as West Coast operations manager for the Armenia Tree Project in Los Angeles before joining AMoA. In her previous role at the museum, she helped secure key works for a landmark Arshile Gorky exhibition and is credited with strengthening the institution's financial sustainability.
