article_text:
The Academy plans to keep taking the Oscars global, from recruiting members in underrepresented countries to streaming the ceremony free on YouTube, its leadership said in Tokyo, where CEO Bill Kramer said the share of members living outside the U.S. has grown from around 5% to 25% in a decade.

Kramer was speaking at an Academy in Tokyo panel at the Tokyo International Film Festival alongside Academy president Lynette Howell Taylor and chief membership, impact and industry officer Meredith Shea, moderated by festival director Hisamatsu Takeo. The festival also presented Kramer with its Global Cinema Leadership Special Award.

Related Stories

Disney Names Carol Choi Asia Pacific President as Luke Kang Retires

Kramer described the membership shift as part of a push for a more diverse and inclusive Academy. A decade ago, he said, only 5% to 6% of members were based outside the U.S. “Now it’s 25%, and that number is growing.” The Academy has about 70 members in Japan.

“People are making movies around the world, people are watching films that are not in their native language more and more,” Kramer said. “We’re making movies everywhere, we’re viewing movies in a much more nimble and accessible way, and the Academy needs to reflect that.”

Kramer pointed out that every category at the most recent Oscars had international representation, including best picture. “Of course, everybody remembers the moment when ‘Parasite’ won. It was sort of a pivot, a shift, I think, in our thinking about what was possible with global cinema at the Oscars, and that continues,” he said, referring to Bong Joon Ho’s 2020 best picture winner.

Howell Taylor explained that besides Oscar nominees, who are automatically put forward, and candidates sponsored by existing members, each branch has an Aperture committee charged with finding filmmakers around the world. “And each year, we have very specific focus for countries that are potentially underrepresented,” she said.

During the audience Q&A, Howell Taylor said: “Just because the membership has increased does not mean that the qualifications have somehow decreased. Our membership was smaller because we were not as global, and we weren’t looking for excellence in filmmakers as much outside of the U.S.”

Over the past couple of years, the Academy has visited India, London, Rio, Morelia, Marrakech and Busan. “We’re thrilled to be here in Tokyo, and you’ll be seeing us do that more and more,” Kramer said, adding that the Academy’s city-by-city member events will continue “all over the world.” This was, he said, the Academy’s “first official Academy trip to the Tokyo Film Festival, but it won’t be our last.”

Being Academy president, Howell Taylor said, “is an incredible privilege because I get to meet storytellers all around the world in this position.” She added: “I carry all the conversations that I have at various film festivals and member gatherings back to L.A. And it’s so crucial to take those conversations and that information because it really does shape the work that the Board does and how our organization moves forward.”

Shea noted that submitting a film for Oscar consideration costs nothing in any category, more than 200 festival awards make short films automatically eligible, and members can watch contenders on the Academy Screening Room app. “That’s our deep commitment to global cinema, that we don’t want individuals to feel like it’s not open, that it is just an L.A.-based, Hollywood-centric organization. The Academy is global, and it welcomes all filmmakers,” she said.

A major step toward a worldwide audience comes with the Oscars’ move to YouTube, where Kramer said the ceremony will be available free to 2.5 billion people in more than 30 languages from 2029. “So, for the first time, everyone around the world will have access to the show at the same time in the same format. And that is a huge, intentional move by the Academy to reach a bigger global audience,” he said.

Asked whether the Tokyo International Film Festival could join the six festivals whose top prizes now qualify films for the international feature race, Kramer said: “We’re looking to expand the number of festivals that help films qualify for the International Feature Film category. That’s a process that we’re undertaking this year, so stay tuned for more information on that.”

In a later answer, Kramer said the first six were chosen in large part on “the timing on the calendar,” and that the Academy is “just beginning these conversations.” Howell Taylor said discussions about expanding the list are “ongoing right now.”

Asked whether the category could one day become redundant as the Academy grows more international, Kramer said: “Right now, I don’t see that category as being redundant.”

Animation is another area where the Academy’s global reach shows. Shea, who ran the animated feature category for more than a decade, said submissions grew from 12 to close to 40 over that period, with at least six anime titles a year. “Japan has such a deep history of animated filmmaking,” said Kramer, who added that the Academy’s globalization “is good for all filmmakers, including Japanese filmmakers.”

Speaking separately with Variety in Tokyo, Kramer, Howell Taylor, Shea and Academy Museum director and president Amy Homma also discussed AI, the festival route into the international feature race and the 2029 YouTube ceremony.

In his closing remarks, Kramer said: “I’m always struck on these trips, and this is no exception, by the warmth, by the sense of community, by the sense of collaboration, and how we all speak the same cinema language. And it’s very heartening, especially in this moment of a lot of global complications and complexities.”

editorial_excerpt_zh: 卢卡·特雷维萨尼将他的变形雕塑与莫罗内厅的文艺复兴壁画联系起来，探索了神圣与世俗、美与腐朽、自然与人造之间的界限。本文题为：圣徒与恐怖：卢卡·特雷维萨尼在维罗纳对物质发起……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "当神圣人物的端庄沉稳遇到不稳定、有机甚至有时令人反胃的物质时，会发生什么？正是在这种对比中——神圣与腐朽相对，美与通常被认为令人不悦的事物相对——维罗纳圣贝尔纳迪诺修道院莫罗内厅举办的卢卡·特雷维萨尼个展《罗莎》（Rosa）拉开了帷幕。展览由卢卡·切里扎（Luca Cerizza）策展，于9月22日至9月22日期间在第二十一届艺术维罗纳（ArtVerona）展会之际举办。与其说这是一个明确的挑衅，不如说该项目构建了对身体和物质两种观念的对质，将质疑形态的所谓稳定以及自然与人工之间界限的任务交给了作品。", "links": [{"text": "ArtVerona", "url": "https://artverona.it/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "语境至关重要：在1494年至1503年间，多梅尼科·莫罗内（Domenico Morone）和他的儿子弗朗切斯科创作了装饰该大厅的壁画，使墙壁上布满了神圣的人物，特雷维萨尼选择与这些人物建立一种与其说直接、不如说建立在张力和对应关系之上的关系。“因此，这并非对话，而是一种温柔的相互挑衅，”艺术家解释道。他挑选了大约20年间创作的二十多件作品，避免聚焦于最著名的作品，以便在自己的研究内部激发更不那么直接的联系。如果说壁画呈现了融入超越性想象的身体，那么特雷维萨尼的雕塑和物品则将人们的注意力带回到存在的物理维度、脆弱性以及贯穿每一个有机体的转化过程中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/ArtVerona_2026_Veronafiere_EnneviFoto_FNT55776-683x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "卢卡·特雷维萨尼，《罗莎》。展览现场，维罗纳圣贝尔纳迪诺修道院莫罗内厅。摄影：Ennevi Foto", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "统一整个展陈的是一条穿过大厅的长长的粉红色底座，上面分布着用不同材料和技术创作的作品，从而催生了一种当代奇观柜（cabinet of curiosities），其中的形态似乎在物体与有机体、建构与恶化之间不断摇摆。植物、面包、铁锈和动物骨骼是艺术家用来探索对环境做出反应、记录时间流逝并逐渐改变其外观的物质的其中一些元素。正是在这个维度中，展览最令人不安的特征浮现了出来：那些看似无定形、脆弱甚至可怕的东西并不是为了产生一种流于形式本身的挑衅效果，而是为了将雕塑带回自然过程的具体性，使其摆脱最终且不可变物体的概念。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因此，与画在墙上的圣徒的对质呈现出一种特殊的强度，因为当神圣的形象倾向于将人物保留在超越时间的象征维度中时，特雷维萨尼的作品却将恰恰逃脱形态控制的东西变得清晰可见。然而，这并不是简单地将精神性与肉体性对立起来，而是去审视物质如何能够成为知识的承载者，即使当它通过脆弱、改变和流失表现出来时也是如此。正如艺术家所观察到的那样，如果在他的研究初期，兴趣主要集中在雕塑的危机及其边界的定义上，那么今天，人们的注意力则集中在材料本身的生命上：“20年前我质问形态；今天我质问物质的生命。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/ArtVerona_2026_Veronafiere_EnneviFoto_FNT55795-683x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "卢卡·特雷维萨尼，《罗莎》。展览现场，维罗纳圣贝尔纳迪诺修道院莫罗内厅。摄影：Ennevi Foto", "credit": "Exibart", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《罗莎》汇集了特雷维萨尼研究的不同阶段，将它们与莫罗内神圣的人物联系在一起，这种对质揭示了永恒与转化之间、身体的理想形象与其不可还原的物质性之间的张力。正是在这种差距中，物质成为了一种知识的工具，它所揭示的不是保持不变的事物，而是不断在成为的事物。", "translated": true}]

Più che una provocazione esplicita, il progetto costruisce un confronto tra due concezioni del corpo e della materia, affidando alle opere il compito di mettere in discussione la presunta stabilità delle forme e il confine tra naturale e artificiale.", "links": [{"text": "ArtVerona", "url": "https://artverona.it/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Il contesto è determinante: tra il 1494 e il 1503, Domenico Morone e il figlio Francesco realizzarono gli affreschi che decorano la sala, popolandone le pareti di figure sacre con le quali Trevisani sceglie di instaurare un rapporto non tanto diretto quanto fondato su tensioni e corrispondenze. «Non un dialogo, quindi, ma una dolce provocazione reciproca», spiega l ’ artista, che ha selezionato oltre venti opere realizzate nell ’ arco di circa vent ’ anni, evitando di concentrarsi sui lavori più noti per far emergere connessioni meno immediate all ’ interno della propria ricerca. article_text:
Cosa accade quando la compostezza delle figure sacre incontra una materia instabile, organica, talvolta persino repellente? Da questo contrasto, in cui il sacro si confronta con il disfacimento e la bellezza con ciò che abitualmente viene considerato sgradevole, si sviluppa Rosa , la mostra personale di Luca Trevisani a cura di Luca Cerizza , allestita nella Sala Morone del Convento di San Bernardino a Verona dal 9 al 22 ottobre, in occasione della ventunesima edizione di ArtVerona . Più che una provocazione esplicita, il progetto costruisce un confronto tra due concezioni del corpo e della materia, affidando alle opere il compito di mettere in discussione la presunta stabilità delle forme e il confine tra naturale e artificiale.

Il contesto è determinante: tra il 1494 e il 1503, Domenico Morone e il figlio Francesco realizzarono gli affreschi che decorano la sala, popolandone le pareti di figure sacre con le quali Trevisani sceglie di instaurare un rapporto non tanto diretto quanto fondato su tensioni e corrispondenze. «Non un dialogo, quindi, ma una dolce provocazione reciproca», spiega l ’ artista, che ha selezionato oltre venti opere realizzate nell ’ arco di circa vent ’ anni, evitando di concentrarsi sui lavori più noti per far emergere connessioni meno immediate all ’ interno della propria ricerca. Se gli affreschi restituiscono corpi inseriti in un immaginario di trascendenza, le sculture e gli oggetti di Trevisani riportano l ’ attenzione sulla dimensione fisica dell ’ esistenza, sulla fragilità e sui processi di trasformazione che investono ogni organismo.

A unificare l ’ allestimento è un lungo plinto dipinto di rosa che attraversa la sala, sul quale si distribuiscono opere realizzate con materiali e tecniche differenti, dando vita a una sorta di gabinetto di curiosità contemporaneo in cui le forme sembrano oscillare continuamente tra oggetto e organismo, costruzione e deterioramento. Piante, pane, ruggine e ossa animali sono alcuni degli elementi attraverso cui l ’ artista indaga una materia che reagisce all ’ ambiente, registra il trascorrere del tempo e modifica progressivamente il proprio aspetto. È proprio in questa dimensione che emerge il carattere più perturbante della mostra: ciò che può apparire informe, fragile o persino orrido non viene utilizzato per produrre un effetto provocatorio fine a sé stesso, ma per riportare la scultura alla concretezza dei processi naturali, sottraendola all ’ idea di un oggetto definitivo e immutabile.

Il confronto con i santi dipinti sulle pareti assume così una particolare intensità, perché, mentre l ’ immagine sacra tende a conservare la figura in una dimensione simbolica che supera il tempo, le opere di Trevisani rendono visibile proprio ciò che sfugge al controllo della forma. Non si tratta, tuttavia, di contrapporre semplicemente spiritualità e corporeità, quanto piuttosto di interrogare il modo in cui la materia possa farsi portatrice di conoscenza, anche quando si manifesta attraverso la fragilità, l ’ alterazione e la perdita. Come osserva l ’ artista, se all ’ inizio della sua ricerca l ’ interesse era rivolto soprattutto alla crisi della scultura e alla definizione dei suoi confini, oggi l ’ attenzione si concentra sulla vita stessa dei materiali: «Vent ’ anni fa interrogavo la forma; oggi interrogo la vita della materia».

Rosa riunisce diversi momenti della ricerca di Trevisani, mettendoli in relazione con le figure sacre di Morone in un confronto che lascia emergere una tensione tra permanenza e trasformazione, tra l ’ immagine ideale del corpo e la sua irriducibile materialità. È in questo scarto che la materia diventa strumento di conoscenza, rivelando non ciò che rimane immutato, ma ciò che, continuamente, diventa.

ビックリするほど当たるためIMA御用達の占い師・マコが、12星座の今をタロット1枚で運気予報！フォトグラファー清水はるみによるファンタスティックな星座＆大アルカナのヴィジュアルと共に、明るい未来の指針を毎月前・後半でお届けします。

11月前半に思うこと

「前略、道の駅より（そいやー！）」

​11月に入り、秋の風が心地よく吹き抜ける季節。私は自他ともに認める無類の「道の駅」好きです。「ちょっとお手洗いをお借りして……」のつもりで立ち寄るのに、帰りには両手いっぱいの新鮮な地場野菜と初産み卵を抱えている。心の中で「そいやっ！」と掛け声を上げながら買い物を楽しむあの空間は、私にとってこの世のパラダイスです。

​先日も和歌山の「道の駅四季の郷公園」と大阪の「道の駅みさき」をハシゴしてきたのですが、この季節のお目当てはなんと言っても……大好物の「無花果（いちじく）」！パックリと割れた甘い完熟無花果を2パック爆買いし、母と二人で心ゆくまで味わう無花果三昧な夜。もう、めちゃくちゃ美味しくて幸せな秋のひとときでした。

​実はこの無花果、スピリチュアル的にも素晴らしいパワーを秘めた果物なのです。​花を外に見せず内側に咲かせる神秘性から「隠された真実」や「直感力」を象徴し、たくさんの実をつける姿は「豊かさ」や「愛と繁栄」を表します。タロットカードで例えるなら、豊穣の「女帝」と、直感と知性の「女教皇」、そして覚醒の「恋人たち」をすべて合わせたような至高の果実！直感力を磨きたい方や、恋する女性にはぜひ食べていただきたい開運フードです。

​ちなみに、道の駅でゲットした元気いっぱいの「ギャル鶏」が産んだ初産み卵は、プリプリの黄身を塩昆布にまぶして一晩寝かせたら最高のお酒のあてに。秋の果物でつくる自家製発酵ドリンクも仕込み中です。

​その土地のエネルギーが詰まった食材を美味しくいただくことこそ、手軽でこの秋最強の開運アクション。​皆様も今週末はお近くの道の駅へ足を延ばして、地球の恵みを心ゆくまで味わってみませんか？

article_text:
The dinosaur market has produced another monster sale.

“Jodi,” a 67-million-year-old Nanotyrannus skeleton, sold Tuesday at Sotheby’s New York for $47.3 million, including fees, more than five times its $9 million high estimate. The skeleton hammered at $40.5 million, making it one of the most expensive dinosaur fossils ever sold at auction.

The result comes just three months after Sotheby’s sold “Gus,” a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton, for a record $50.1 million . That July sale, which carried a $20 million–$30 million estimate, established a new high for prehistoric fossils, surpassing the $44.6 million paid for the Stegosaurus “Apex” in 2024. Jodi came remarkably close to that record, despite being considerably smaller and lacking the brand recognition of a T. rex .

The nearly 20-foot-long skeleton was discovered in Montana’s Hell Creek Formation in 2019 by rancher Jodi Pierson, for whom the fossil was named. According to Sotheby’s, it’s one of only three known Nanotyrannus skeletons and includes 191 fossil bone elements, among them a nearly complete skull.

Until recently, scientists weren’t even sure Nanotyrannus was a separate dinosaur. For decades, researchers debated whether the smaller predator was simply a juvenile T. rex . A study published in Nature last year helped settle the argument, identifying Nanotyrannus as a distinct genus that lived alongside its much larger cousin.

Jodi has already had something of a career in the art market . In 2023, when it was known as “Chomper” and still identified as a juvenile T. rex , London dealer David Aaron offered it for $20 million at Frieze Masters. (The work didn’t sell then as the current consignor acquired it in 2021, according to Sotheby’s provenance listing .) Three years later, with a new name and a new scientific identity, it has sold for more than twice that amount.

The sale is just more evidence that dinosaurs have become serious trophy objects for wealthy collectors, joining blue-chip paintings, rare watches, and sports memorabilia at the top end of the luxury market. In recent years, prices have climbed at a remarkable pace. Christie’s sold the T. rex “Stan” for $31.8 million in 2020, while a juvenile Ceratosaurus brought $30.5 million at Sotheby’s last year against an estimate of just $4 million–$6 million.

The boom has also raised concerns among paleontologists , who worry that scientifically important fossils are increasingly being priced beyond the reach of museums and disappearing into private collections. Auction houses counter that private investment helps fund the expensive work of excavating, preserving, and studying specimens.

article_text:
This year’s Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) attracted more than 275,000 visitors across screenings of 315 films (94 of them world premieres) and special events. Guests included Alfonso Cuarón, Michelle Yeoh, Koreeda Hirokazu, Ann Hui, Fan Bingbing, and many more.

Headed by Zhang Yimou, the competition jury awarded best film to Majid Majidi’s Midday Meal , a piercing Iranian drama about a teacher’s efforts to keep a school open. This was the first year BIFF was classified as an “A” list festival, making Midday Meal eligible for Academy Award shortlisting.

The legendary Chinese star Zhou Xun won a best actor award for The First Taste of Loneliness , which also won an Artistic Contribution prize. Sailesh Rathnakumar’s Selvi , which screened in BIFF’s Vision section, won two awards: Hylife Vision and Taipei Film Commission. The long tail of Payal Kapadia’s All We Imagine as Light hangs over Selvi , a close-up account of a healthcare worker’s unraveling. Producer Anjali Patil stars in the title role as a hard-working health practitioner forced to undergo double and triple shifts to protect her suicidal sister.

Director Rathnakumar follows Selvi throughout a tough, unforgiving city as she takes overloaded buses, trains, and scooters to her appointments. Her clients require constant attention, shown in uncomfortable detail. (For example: here’s how you clean a tracheotomy tube.) Just as difficult are her bosses reaping profits from untenable work schedules. She lives in a hostel shared with other health workers, where there is no privacy and usually no running water. Selvi also has to send money home to a mother who constantly criticizes her.

Selvi

Selvi can be a tough slog, although Patil gives a determined and appealing performance. Rathnakumar doesn’t have much to say about the healthcare crisis other than the system being broken. It’s a worldwide problem that deserves attention, but a topic that needs a strong script. This story devolves into soap-opera melodrama involving unwanted pregnancies and cheating lovers.

On the opposite spectrum from Selvi ‘s carefully traditional filmmaking style is Arvin Belarmino’s feature debut Ria , a defiantly provocative tour through a Filipino underworld of rappers, bikers, squatters, and scavengers. It opens with a blistering punk rock tirade against society—”Burn the state, crush the state, serve it on a plate”—delivered in a full-throttled roar by the title character, a bitter, sullen young woman played with uncommon skill by Nour Hooshmand. A Filipino–Iranian actor, Hooshmand also appears in Filipiñana . Ringed with kohl, her enormous eyes project equal parts hostility and despair.

Ria lives in a condemned tenement slated for development by a realtor who hires goons to disrupt the punk community. It’s an urban wasteland rendered more unlivable when water and electricity are shut down. Arson burns down the commune headquarters, almost killing a hungover musician. Ria cares for her adoptive mother Olga, who is slowly succumbing to diabetes. Ria works as a chambermaid in a luxury hotel, stealing liquor and toiletries and sneaking cold-water washes in sinks. Her paycheck goes to Olga’s insulin, but her friend still faces the amputation of her foot, an operation no one can afford.

One possible solution is to work in porn with her friend Kim in secret productions arranged through the hospital. Ria offers to be an assistant, but in a cringe-inducing scene her boss says he only wants performers. Her head in her hands, Ria later stares out a window at the city at night. It’s a moment heartbreaking in its simplicity.

Belarmino’s style is loud and in-your-face. In his debut feature, nothing is sacred, anything can be mocked, and life itself feels worthless. It’s an admirably hard-edged story that slips into sentimentality at the worst possible moments, only to be redeemed by frequent musical passages and Hooshmand’s expert performance.

Working with a tiny budget, the director stages some impressively large-scale street riots, punks firebombing police vans and showering riot cops with bodily fluids. Knowing they can’t win doesn’t stop them from trying, despite bullets and explosions. To Belarmino’s credit, he delivers an uncompromising ending. Ria had its world-premiere screening in the Vision section, where Belarmino appeared in person. He was engaging and outgoing, despite suffering a detached retina on his arrival that left him sporting a padded eyepatch.

Earbug

Another Vision world premiere had a similar DIY vibe. Earbug , Kim Hyomi’s feature-directing debut, is a deliberately low-res animation about twenty-something artists on the cusp of failure. Compared to Disney output, Earbug is a visual mess, its frames shimmering like a wavering Internet signal. Digital artifacts abound, hair doesn’t move, characters shuffle awkwardly when walking, sets are poorly designed and lit, and at times Hyomi just gives up and substitutes in actual film footage for drawing.

Two aspiring artists live in a cramped apartment. Kim Jeong-yeon wants to be a writer, but is worried that she doesn’t have enough life experience. Kim Na-jeong, a painter, mocks Jeong-yeon’s attempts to write about love, laughing that she’s asexual.

The premise of Jeon-yeon’s novel is that an alien has come to Earth searching for true, absolute love. Judges at her school critique her writing mercilessly, one calling for a more active protagonist, the other saying it’s all too impersonal. Jeon-yeon doubts herself so much that she starts missing writing deadlines.

She works at the convenience store chain Nice to EU (a play on Korea’s ubiquitous Nice to CU stores), giving outdated food to a beggar who drops by nightly. That gets her fired, setting off more remorse. On top of that, her suicidal father keeps texting that he’s going to kill himself. Jeon-yeon is furious when Na-jeong has an affair with a married curator in order to get a solo show at a gallery. Na-jeong moves out, leaving Jeon-yeon nothing but empty walls and spiraling depression.

Hyomi, who also wrote and edited Earbug , takes her movie into decidedly offbeat territory when she describes Jeon-yeon’s sci-fi novel. The alien takes the form of an earwig in order to travel from host to host. Occasionally he will appear life-size to criticize his creator’s writing. Another narrative strand involves teen rockers who enrage a local minister after he finds them practicing in his church. At one point, a severed ear turns into a giant UFO that might be spreading a pneumonia virus that has shut down the city.

Although its story is scattered and animation primitive, Earbug captures the struggle young artists face as they fail repeatedly in their efforts. With nothing to encourage continuing, their perseverance becomes admirable. In a similar way, Hyomi has succeeded in completing a feature despite everything against her. Well, not everything: her film was supported in part by the Korean Academy of Film Arts. Like the two directors above, she is a talent still in development.

article_text:
Paul Bettany opened up in a recent interview with The Times about the public’s misconception of his relationship with Johnny Depp after text messages between the two actors were used in court during Depp’s libel lawsuit against The Sun.

“I hadn’t spoken to Johnny in years when that happened and I haven’t spoken to him since. I was being painted as this close friend of a guy I hadn’t spoken to in years and, honestly, amid all the shit two celebrities threw at each other, that bit was the most odd,” Paul told the publication.

Popular on Variety

“So I decided to say nothing because, I think, people know me,” he continued. “I’ve been married 23 years and, for what I do, I live an incredibly quiet life. Everybody kind of thought this is probably a nothing burger – and left it alone.”

In 2013, a controversial text exchange between Depp and Bettany became public when it was read during a Feb. 2020 trial hearing. “Let’s burn Amber!!!” wrote Depp, to which Bettany responded: “Having thought it through I don’t think we should burn Amber – she’s delightful company and easy on the eye, plus I’m not sure she’s a witch. We could of course try the English course of action in these predicaments ­– we do a drowning test. Thoughts?” Depp responded that they should “drown her before we burn her!!! I will fuck her burnt corpse afterwards to make sure she’s dead.”

The two actors worked together on multiple films, including 2010’s “The Tourist,” 2014’s “Transcendence” and 2015’s “Mortdecai.”

Depp initially sued News Group Newspapers (NGN) (which publishes The Sun) for libel after an article was published by the publication titled “Gone Potty – How can JK Rowling be ‘genuinely happy’ casting wife beater Johnny Depp in the new ‘Fantastic Beasts’ film?” Depp alleged that the article “caused serious harm to (his) personal and professional reputation” and also caused him “significant distress and embarrassment.” In 2020, Judge Andrew Nicol ruled against Depp.

article_text:
Across the more than 170 exhibitors, the 2026 edition of Frieze London features a diverse array of works from mixed-media installations to textiles drawing on Indigenous weaving traditions to found objects to interactive digital works to works on paper. Throughout the aisles, visitors will find work by artists engaging a range of themes in their work, including climate change, the human life cycle, the destructive nature of AI, and more.

Below, a look at the 10 best booths at Frieze London, which runs through October 18 at Regent’s Park.

Emma Stibbon at Cristea Roberts Gallery Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews Emma Stibbon engages directly with climate change through a site-specific installation that brings the rocky cliffs of the British coastline to the Frieze tent. Her nearly 10-foot-tall, mixed-media work, Rock Fall, Bideford Bay (2025), is stabilized by a collection of rocks gathered from Green Cliff in North Devon that have been spread across the floor. Using pigments ground from sandstone, clay, shale, and limestone found on the beaches of Norfolk, Dorset, and Sussex, Stibbon paints the landscape with its own materials, documenting the rapid coastal erosion along UK coastlines. The work links melting polar ice and rising sea levels to local habitats, showing that environmental collapse isn’t only a distant threat. This climate urgency continues across her other drawings on view, like Seaford Head, Sussex (2026) and Fallen Fence Happisburgh (2026). Stibbon transforms these vanishing geological archives into artwork that brings our ongoing climate crisis much closer to home.

Jun Martinez at Cecilia Brunson Projects Image Credit: Courtesy the artist and Cecilia Brunson Projects At the center of Cecilia Brunson’s booth is Jun Martínez’s five-panel painting On Disturbed Land and Abandoned Pastures (Roble Blanco del Caribe) I-III (2026). Dominated by a vivid blue background with touches of purple, white, green, and brown, it depicts the leaves and flowers of the roble blanco tree. For Martínez, this tree serves as both an aesthetic subject and a symbol of Caribbean ecological survival and renewal. By framing his native Puerto Rico and its fragile biodiversity against the pressures of modern ecosystems and its relationship to the US, the artist treats the natural landscape as a living, active archive of resilience rather than a passive backdrop. Now based in London, Martínez often explores memory, perception, and landscape in his work, which act as sites where histories of colonialism can be remembered, balancing local observation with painterly traditions.

Eilen Itzel do Espírito Santo at Bolanle Contemporary Image Credit: Linda Nylind/Courtesy Frieze Afro-Dominican artist Eilen Itzel do Espírito Santo makes her Frieze debut in the Artist-to-Artist section, selected by Firelei Báez. Her immersive installation, which feature red flooring and soft pink walls, explores the cycle of life and death, bridging physical creation with the spiritual labor of the womb. Do Espírito Santo incorporates tropical Caribbean elements into her works, pairing vibrant paintings with sculptures crafted from cement, soil, clay, and twigs. Her project is rooted in communal memory and channels ancestral spirits, as well as her relationship with Obàtálá, the Yoruba deity of creation. The pieces draw a poetic parallel between the artist and the snail, an animal associated with Obàtálá as a natural mark-maker who leaves traces of its movements. Through her art, do Espírito Santo honors different ways of being within the African diaspora, highlighting the resilience needed to survive despite colonialism.

Jayeeta Chatterjee at Chemould CoLab Image Credit: Linda Nylind/Courtesy Frieze Indian artist Jayeeta Chatterjee presents an exploration of gendered labor and agency through an intricate multimedia textile installation. At the heart of her display is The Infinite Weft (2026), a monumental tapestry made from woodcut prints on recycled saris, stitched using Nakshi Kantha, a traditional Bengali quilting and embroidery technique now facing extinction. Hand-sewn, the work reflects the complex, non-linear roles women navigate across work, family, and domestic life. During a residency in Hampi, on the southwestern coast of India, Chatterjee photographed the women who work at the Bonkai weaving center, capturing their historic step towards financial independence. By printing her compositions onto used saris sourced directly from her subjects, the artist embeds these women’s daily realities in the fabric itself. Chatterjee adds recording marks of the women’s voices, translating their conversations into embroidered audio waveforms. The work’s compositions reflect the repetition of domestic chores and the tight-knit, alternative social sanctuary these weavers create together, making their invisible histories visible.

Payne Zhu at Spurs Gallery Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews Anal Intelligence is certainly a provocative title for this installation by Shanghai-born artist Payne Zhu, whose practice looks at AI through the visceral lens of the human digestive system. Featuring two paintings and an eight-channel, real-time-rendered video, the presentation tackles themes of overconsumption and digital gluttony. Zhu’s installation combines familiar, hyper-stimulating viral clips, such as those seen in YouTube mukbang eating videos, fashion hauls, and pop music videos, with drone footage and game-engine software. By editing this chaotic media stream, the artist creates a case that modern artificial intelligence is driven not by intelligence but by a gluttonous process of destruction and data digestion. In today’s often troubling digital landscape, human actions and emotions are reduced to “turbid matter” extracted to feed an insatiable, endless network. Through this technological mismatch, Zhu transforms the booth into an eerie, consumerist loop where production becomes digestion becomes production again, interrogating how our digital behavior consumes itself.

Cynthia Talmadge at Ellie Rines Gallery Image Credit: Emi Eleode for ARTnews New York–based artist Cynthia Talmadge’s immersive installation, Mitford/Soong , examines two prominent 20th century socialite dynasties, the British Mitfords and the Chinese Soongs. At first glance, her four paintings evoke an Art Deco aesthetic, but on closer inspection they reveal detailed, grainy pointillist brushwork. Rendered in a dark, vignetted palette, these works mimic vintage film stills, incorporating dramatic Dutch angles and hard shadows to create a cinematic horror narrative. Drawing on German Expressionism and early Chinese film, Talmadge links these two groups of women through historical trauma, gender, and soft power. Surrounded by custom wallpaper and eight trompe l’œil pinboard paintings that function as psychological self-portraits, the booth collapses domestic intimacy and historical cruelty into a theatrical study with complex, interwoven themes.

Denzil Forrester at Thaddaeus Ropac Image Credit: ©Denzil Forrest/Courtesy the artist and Thaddaeus Ropac Two large-scale oil paintings by Denzil Forrester radiate liveliness and movement that immediately catch the eye. They present the nightclub as a space for joy, music, and spiritual fulfillment, while also reflecting underlying political friction and nostalgia. In Professor Version (2025), Forrester captures the dancehall’s vibrant energy, depicting four figures in motion across the floor, with two DJs commanding the decks in the background. By contrast, Yard (2025) illustrates a scene where uniformed police with pointed helmets disrupt a yard party, circling the DJ who spins the deck at the center of the room. Both works display jewel-shaped geometry, with strobe lights fracturing the details into diamond-like shapes that create a dreamlike ambiguity. Influenced by his current home in Cornwall and memories of Grenada and Rome, Forrester uses a color palette of purples, warm ambers, and icy blues. By remixing figures from his own archive, much like a reggae dub DJ remixes tracks, Forrester conveys gesture, action, and the lasting tension of city life.

Selma Selman at acb Gallery Image Credit: Photo Linda Nylind/Courtesy Frieze Contemporary Bosnian artist Selma Selman showcases a melancholic collection of paintings and texts created on discarded metal objects, car parts, and a bathtub. As a member of the Roma community in Bosnia and Herzegovina, she repurposes these materials to challenge how modern society assigns value to physical objects, labor, and marginalized communities. When she was 26 years old, she founded an organization dedicated to the education and empowerment of young Roma girls. Through her expressive brushwork, she turns scrap metal into a canvas for personal and political expression, infusing industrial waste with emotional depth. Her artistic practice spans performance, painting, and social activism, elevating recycled materials into art. Featured in the new curated section “The Code Universe, led by Carol Yinghua Lu, Selman’s installation critiques capitalist and cultural hierarchies at the fair, highlighting the tension between economic survival and artistic value.

Juan Uslè at Frith Street Gallery Image Credit: Ben Westoby, Fine Art Documentation/Courtesy the artist and Firth Street Gallery. Between Steps , an immersive, room-size display by Spanish painter Juan Uslé, showcases a rhythmic, personal evolution in his work. This project invites viewers into an interactive environment that interweaves 12 paintings with 210 photographs, arranged above and below a two-tone wall in deep purple and white. The exhibit is designed to be experienced as a visual poem, with the sequenced imagery echoing the steady rhythm of a beating pulse, human breath, or a leisurely walk. Captured in locations such as London, New York, and his hometown of Saro in northern Spain, Uslé’s photographs document fleeting, everyday urban encounters with a touch of abstraction. Rather than translating images onto the painted canvas, he creates a dialogue between the two mediums to narrow the gap between reality and fiction. By combining these photographic impressions with his painterly style, Uslé encourages us to slow down and appreciate the subtle, hidden meanings within our ever-changing modern surroundings.

Arébénor Basséne at Selebe Yoon Image Credit: Tom Carter/Courtesy the artist and Selebe Yoon Presenting a captivating series of five paintings, Senegalese artist Arébénor Basséne combines Dogon (an Indigenous ethnic group in Mali) cosmology with human history. The works move between microscopic details and broad bird’s-eye views, as Basséne uses natural pigments, gum arabic, wood shavings, and sand to explore the cosmos. His paintings resemble celestial constellations and archaeological maps, inspired by historical cartographers such as the Greco-Roman Ptolemy and 12th century cartographer al-Idrisi, representing both real and fictional worlds. While one painting is reminiscent of an ancient map, using swirling compositions that highlight movement, like the eye of an approaching storm on a modern-day weather forecast, another has underwater scenes. Through this layering, Basséne looks to the spiritual and astronomical knowledge of the Sahel, a biogeographical region in Africa that references the star Sirius as an ancestral guide. After recently exhibiting with the Pinault Collection, his Frieze London debut of textured topographies blurs the boundaries between spirit and science, analyzing how ancient African calendars and star charts confront Western anthropological biases.

article_text:
Dylan Skolnick is returning as Director of the Cinema Arts Centre following protests and boycotts over his firing.

In a post announcing Skolnick’s reinstatement, the Long Island cultural institution said that its board of directors had sat down for a series of meetings with an independent mediator. “Those discussions have resulted in an agreement to move forward together, and we are pleased to welcome Dylan back to the Cinema,” the announcement read.

In September, Skolnick was ousted by the CAC board of directors for “serious misconduct.” In justifying the move, the organization slammed Skolnick as a “dysfunctional” and “disloyal” manager whose freelance work as a film buyer for other indie cinemas was a conflict of interest. Skolnick and his supporters countered that the CAC board was experiencing a “hostile takeover” and said that his moonlighting as a film buyer was common practice in the business. Skolnick said he had informed an earlier iteration of the board of his work, but conceded that the current leadership was unaware of his side gig.

Skolnick had deep ties to the institution, which his parents had founded in Huntington, New York more than 50 years ago, as well as strong connections to the wider filmmaking world. Major figures such as Edie Falco, Kent Jones, and Isabella Rossellini leapt to his support, while donations to the CAC dried up, and box office receipts cratered, IndieWire reported last month.

The CAC said that as part of Skolnick’s reinstatement, a new co-director will be hired in the coming months to help lead the organization and its board will invite several new members, “including individuals with backgrounds and experience in the film world.” Skolnick and his fellow co-director and and the CAC board will “undergo additional training focused on effective governance, leadership, accountability and fostering a positive workplace culture.”

In a statement, the CAC leadership acknowledged the fissures created by Skolnick’s ouster, as well as the need to repair relationships and address the non-profit’s financial challenges.

“We want to extend our deepest gratitude to everyone who spoke up, showed their support, and stood by the Cinema during one of the most challenging periods in its history,” the theater said in a statement. “Your voices made a difference, and your continued commitment to this institution means more than we can express.”

Im Roman ist das etwas anderes: Man kann hin- und herblättern und weiß dann ungefähr wieder Bescheid. Also habe ich zunächst ausprobiert, ob sich die Geschichte chronologisch erzählen lässt und welche Elemente man dafür beibehalten müsste. Das habe ich schon vor vier oder fünf Jahren gemacht, bevor ich mich überhaupt nach den Rechten für das Buch erkundigt hatte. Ich sagte zu Jenny Erpenbeck: „Gib mir mal etwas Zeit, damit ich das ausprobieren kann, bevor ich Geld für die Option bezahle.“ Das hat sie gemacht, und sie war dann auch überrascht: „Ja, man kann das ja chronologisch erzählen.“ Sie meinte, sie selbst habe die Geschichte nur so erzählen können, wie sie sie erzählt hat. Nachdem sie mir also den Freibrief gegeben hatte, die Geschichte so umzukrempeln, war eigentlich alles bereit.

Was ist noch neu im Film?

Schlöndorff: Der Roman hat keine Dialoge. Davor hatte ich aber nie Angst. Was die Figuren zueinander sagen, fällt einem dann schon ein. Es braucht auch nicht viel. Es soll ja nicht reflektiert werden; es geht um das Alltägliche.

Warum haben Sie in einem so emblematischen Gebäude wie Einsteins Sommerhaus gedreht? War das eine Produktionsentscheidung oder auch inhaltlich für den Film wichtig?

Schlöndorff: Beim Lesen fragt man sich natürlich: Wo könnte ich das drehen? Ich bin dann mit dem Motorboot verschiedene Seen abgefahren. Die Häuser, die ich vom See aus gesehen habe, gefielen mir alle nicht besonders. Dann dachte ich: „Eigentlich müsste es so ein Haus sein wie Einsteins Haus in Caputh. Das kenne ich, weil ich in der Nähe lebe und schon öfter dort war. Aber dort zu drehen, ist bestimmt völlig unmöglich – das ist ja ein historisches Denkmal.“ Dann stellte sich aber heraus, dass man beim Einstein-Forum sehr aufgeschlossen war. Dort sagte man, Einstein habe nie gewollt, dass das Haus ein Museum wird, sondern dass es ein lebendiger Ort bleibt. Dort finden auch Seminare statt, und es kommen Studierende aus der ganzen Welt. Es war also ein Glücksfall, dass wir das Haus nicht nur von außen, sondern auch von innen nutzen durften. Die Badewanne, auf deren Rand Susanne Wolff als Frau des Architekten sitzt, ist tatsächlich Albert Einsteins Badewanne. Einstein ließ sein Haus von einem jungen Architekten mit neuen Ideen bauen. Drei oder vier Jahre später kamen die Nazis an die Macht, und Einstein musste das Haus verlassen. Dann zog dort die Hitlerjugend ein – oder zunächst irgendwelche Nazi-Tiere. Später besetzte die Rote Armee das Haus und stellte vierzig Pferde in den Garten. Schließlich kamen verdiente Antifaschisten: ein Schriftsteller-Ehepaar, das vor den Nazis nach Moskau geflohen war und dann zurückkam, um den Sommer in diesem Haus zu verbringen und zu schreiben. Mit der Wende meldeten sich dann wieder die Erstbesitzer, die inzwischen im Rheinland und in der Schweiz lebten. Die Geschichte von Einsteins Haus und die des Hauses im Roman weisen also viele Überschneidungen auf.

Die Figur des Architekten bekommt etwas sehr Dunkles, wenn man die Baupläne für Lagerbaracken auf seinem Schreibtisch sieht.

Schlöndorff: Man könnte sagen, dass es in dem Film viele Fundstücke gibt. Das Haus selbst ist ein Fundstück: dass es da war, dass ich es kannte und dass wir es nutzen durften. Der Architekt des Einstein-Hauses, Konrad Wachsmann , experimentierte mit Fertigbauweisen aus Holz. Eine Firma in Sachsen baute das Haus für Einstein. Später errichtete dieselbe Firma mit derselben Methode Baracken für Lager. Sie stellte uns aus ihrem Archiv das Modell der Baracke zur Verfügung, das man im Film sieht, sowie die Pläne für die Reichsarbeitsdienst-Baracken. Zunächst waren es Baracken für den Reichsarbeitsdienst, später für Gefangene und schließlich für Konzentrationslager. Tatsächlich ergab sich das eine aus dem anderen. Man könnte also beinahe von einer Linie sprechen, die – architektonisch gesehen – vom Bauhaus bis ins Konzentrationslager führt, aber auch zur Fertigbauweise der DDR. Der Architekt war aus den USA zurückgekommen und hatte sich angesehen, wie in der DDR Wohnungen aus Fertigteilen – den sogenannten Platten – gebaut wurden.

Ist dieses Haus am See Heimat oder nur ein Ort für den Sommerurlaub?

Schlöndorff: Ich glaube, dass alle, die wir zeigen, das Haus als ein Stück Heimat betrachten. Das gilt zunächst für die Bauerntochter, deren Mitgift es sein sollte. Dann für den Architekten, der das Grundstück mit seiner Frau entdeckt und sagt: „Hier könnten wir glücklich sein.“ Und schließlich für die jüdische Familie, die sich sagt: „Hier könnten wir unsere Sommer verbringen.“ So wird das Haus für alle zu dem, was man Heimat nennt. Alle glauben, an einem bestimmten Ort glücklich werden zu können. Sie rechnen nicht damit, dass die Weltgeschichte weitergeht – ganz gleich, an welchem Ort man ist. Und dass man nichts festhalten kann. Mir selbst ist der Begriff „Heimat“ irgendwie verdächtig; er ist ja auch völkisch missbraucht worden. Und dann gab es den Heimatfilm, der auch nicht gerade mein filmisches Vorbild ist. Aber genau das zu reflektieren, ist ein zentrales Thema: Wie viel liegt am Ort, und wie viel eigentlich an den Menschen selbst?

Thomas Mann schreibt in den „Buddenbrooks“, dass der Tod kommt, wenn das Haus fertig ist. Am Ende Ihres Films – und auch des Romans – stirbt das Haus. Wie wäre „Heimsuchung“ nach dem Abriss des Hauses weitergegangen? Was hält die Generationen dann noch zusammen?

Schlöndorff: Ja, das ist ganz klar: Für den Verkauf bekommen sie irgendwie 18.000 Ostmark. Das Haus wird abgerissen, und das Grundstück ist dann zwei Millionen Euro wert. Ich stelle mir vor, dass dort Ferienapartments gebaut werden, fünf Stockwerke hoch. So etwas kann man sich an allen möglichen Seeufern anschauen. In Bad Saarow am Scharmützelsee hat Chipperfield eine Ferienanlage gebaut; dort liegen die Quadratmeterpreise bei etwa 10.000 bis 12.000 Euro.

Im Scharmützelsee spiegelt sich die Weltgeschichte, aber die findet anderswo statt, und die Menschen am See erleben nur deren Folgen. Wie kann man heute überhaupt noch Geschichte im Film erzählen?

Schlöndorff: Ich habe immer zu Jenny Erpenbeck gesagt: „Du hast mir eine großartige Vorlage geliefert, mit der ich mich in vielem identifizieren konnte.“ Ich bin zum Beispiel buchstäblich in einer dieser Baracken aufgewachsen, die nach der Ausbombung Wiesbadens als Behelfsheim im Taunus aufgebaut worden waren. Natürlich kam nie einer der Großen der Welt dorthin. Aber wir wussten genau – ich bin 1939 geboren und kam 1944 dorthin –, wer die Nazis waren. Das spürte man bei den Nachbarn und im Umfeld, bei denen, die das Sagen hatten. Und man spürte auch, wie einem allmählich der Boden unter den Füßen weggerissen wurde, wie eine Besatzungsmacht ankam und danach eine andere Art zu leben, ein anderes System – eben die Bundesrepublik – Einzug hielt. Die großen geschichtlichen Ereignisse waren also auch in diesem Dorf zu spüren. Das Spannende ist, die Geschichte gewissermaßen von unten zu erzählen. Einerseits erzählt sich Geschichte durch die Natur und die Jahreszeiten. Daran erkennt man, wie die Jahre vergehen: Plötzlich liegt Schnee, dann blühen die Bäume, die Kirschen werden geerntet, und schließlich ist wieder Herbst. Die Natur verändert sich ständig, und daran spürt man, wie die Zeit vergeht. Andererseits wird der Film natürlich von den Schauspielern getragen – nicht vom Ort oder vom Haus, sondern von fünf, sechs oder noch mehr starken Schauspielpersönlichkeiten, die zusammen beinahe meine Familie sind. Mit fast allen hatte ich schon gearbeitet: mit Angela Winkler 50 Jahre lang, mit anderen kürzer. Nur mit Lars Eidinger hatte ich noch nicht gearbeitet. Ich hatte ihn aber seit 20 Jahren am Theater hier in Berlin beobachtet und ihn auch sonst oft getroffen. Von Anfang an herrschte eine große Vertrautheit und Selbstverständlichkeit darin, wie die Schauspieler ihre Rollen und das Grundstück angenommen haben. Ich glaube, alle hatten irgendwie das Gefühl, zu Hause zu sein.

„Heimsuchung“ ist in vielen Bundesländern mittlerweile Pflichtlektüre für das Abitur. Was wollen Sie mit dem Film den Jüngeren vermitteln?

Schlöndorff: Als wir angefangen haben, wussten wir das noch nicht. Aber das ist natürlich ganz toll, denn dann weiß man schon einmal: Es gibt junge Zuschauer, denen der Film vielleicht dabei hilft, die Geschichte zu verstehen. Und vielleicht hilft er ihnen auch zu verstehen, was ein Film ist – im Unterschied zu einem literarischen Werk. Ich will ihnen nicht unbedingt deutsche Geschichte beibringen. Ich bin schon froh, wenn ich sie für die Filmkunst sensibilisieren kann – wenn sie den Prozess beobachten können: „Ach, hier ist das Buch, durch das wir uns im Deutschunterricht quälen müssen, und hier ist der Film, vor den wir uns einfach bequem setzen können. Wie ist es denn von dem einen zum anderen gekommen?“ Vielleicht werden sie so zu guten Zuschauerinnen und Zuschauern – jetzt und auch in Zukunft.

Buch und Film fassen mit fast traumwandlerischer Sicherheit nahezu 100 Jahre deutscher Geschichte zusammen – ohne die klassischen historischen Bezugspunkte.

Schlöndorff: Für mich sollte es nie einen Bruch geben. Deshalb gibt es im Film auch keine Jahreszahlen. Nur drei Mal greife ich auf Wochenschauaufnahmen zurück: 1936 die Olympischen Spiele – aha, die Nazis sind an der Regierung. 1945 das zerstörte Berlin – aha, der Krieg ist vorbei, die Russen sind da. Und dann, 1989, fällt die Mauer, und die Besitzverhältnisse im Osten werden umgekrempelt. Mehr sollte es nicht sein. Dazwischen sind alle Übergänge fließend. Im Rückblick erkennt man historische Einschnitte. Aber während man die Geschichte erlebt, geht ein Tag in den nächsten über – mehr nicht.

Ein Tag geht in den nächsten über. Wie schätzen Sie die gegenwärtige politische Situation ein?

Schlöndorff: Na ja, etwas kann sich ganz schleichend verändern, ohne dass man die Übergänge bemerkt. Im Rückblick sieht es dann vielleicht aus wie ein Erdbeben, obwohl es im jeweiligen Augenblick nur eine kleine Erschütterung war: „Aha, die Wahlergebnisse haben sich verändert.“ Dabei geschieht Gewaltiges. Man sollte sich bewusst machen, dass die Welt, wie sie heute ist, nicht immer so bleiben wird. Ich habe darauf einen Einfluss – einen sehr geringen, aber ich muss mir zumindest bewusst sein, dass sich die Dinge verändern. Orientierungslosigkeit ist nichts Neues. Die Menschen wissen nicht, wohin es geht, und fühlen sich verängstigt. Dabei haben sie noch nie gewusst, was kommt: In den 1920er-Jahren wussten sie nicht, dass die Nazis an die Macht kommen würden. Während der NS-Zeit wussten sie nicht, dass der Krieg verloren gehen würde. Nach dem verlorenen Krieg war ungewiss, wohin der Wiederaufbau führen würde, und beim Fall der Mauer wusste man nicht, was die Wiedervereinigung bringen würde. Die Zukunft ist immer offen, deshalb muss man keine Angst vor ihr haben. Man erlebt sie einen Tag nach dem anderen. Diese Ruhe versuche ich mit dem Film zu vermitteln. Nichts davon ist einen großen Aufstand wert. Man muss einfach hinnehmen, dass alles vergänglich ist – nicht nur für die Buddhisten, sondern auch für uns.

我出生于1939年,到1944年 - 谁是纳粹。有人在邻居和周围,在那些有说话的人,也感觉到一个逐渐地下地被切断,一个占领力量到来,然后生活的另一种方式,另一个系统 - 正是联邦共和国 - 进入。季节是如何流逝的:突然下雪,树木开花,草莓种植,最后又是秋天,自然不断变化,你感觉到时间流逝的样子,另一方面,电影当然是由演员带来的 - 不是从地方或房子,而是由五个,六个或更多强大的演员,几乎是我的家人在一起,我已经与几乎所有人一起工作:与安吉拉·温克勒50年,与其他更短的,只有与拉斯·艾丁格,我还没有工作,但我已经在柏林剧院观看了20年,也经常见到他,从一开始,演员们如何接受他们的角色和财产的认识和自觉,我认为每个人都有一种感觉在家里。", "links": [{"text": "Angela Winkler", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/person/details/83306/angela-winkler"}, {"text": "Lars Eidinger", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/person/details/225103/lars-eidinger"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“家居寻找”在许多联邦国家现在是必备的读书,你想用这部电影向年轻人传达什么?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Schlöndorff:当我们开始的时候,我们还不知道这一点,但这当然是很棒的,因为那时你就知道:有年轻观众,这部电影可能会帮助他们了解故事,也许这部电影也会帮助他们了解电影是什么,与文学作品不同,我不一定会教他们德国历史,我很高兴能让他们对电影艺术感知,如果他们能观察这个过程,我会说:“哦,这里就是这部电影。这本书,我们必须在德语学习中受苦,这就是我们可以轻松地坐下的电影,怎么会从一个到另一个?”也许他们会成为好观众,现在和未来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/bild/filmdb/379702/volker-schlondorff-heimsuchung.jpg?t=1791965709", "alt": "“家居”的“家居”", "caption": "与他的集合:Susanne Wolff(L.),Martina Gedeck(第2版)和Lars Eidinger(第2版)(© imago/Future Image)", "credit": "Filmdienst", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "图书和电影与几乎梦想变化的安全结合了近100年的德国历史 - 没有经典的历史参考点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于我来说,从来不应该有破裂,这就是为什么电影中也没有年度数字,我只用三次来回复周刊录像: 1936 奥林匹克运动会:纳粹在政府上。 1945 柏林被摧毁,哈哈,战争结束了,俄罗斯人来了。 1989 城墙倒下,东方的财产关系被逆转。 更多不应该是。在回眼中,你会发现历史的缩写,但当你经历历史时,一天会转向下一天,再也不会。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "下一篇:你现在的政治状况如何看待?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Schlöndorff:好吧,有些事情可以完全变动,没有注意到过渡。在后面看,它可能看起来像一个地震,尽管在某个时刻,它只是一个小震动:“哦,选举结果已经改变了。是,事情发生了变化,不方向性是什么新鲜事,人们不知道走向哪里,感到害怕,他们从来没有知道什么会发生。 1920 那一年,他们不知道纳粹会掌权,在纳粹时代,他们不知道战争会失去,在失去的战争之后,不确定重建会导致什么,而在墙壁倒塌时,他们知道。未來的將會帶來什麼? 未來總是開放的,所以你不必害怕它,你會經歷它一日一日,我試圖用電影傳達這種安靜,沒有什麼值得一場大反抗,你只需要承認,一切都是暫時的,不僅是佛教徒,而且是我們。", "translated": true}]
excerpt_original: In ihrem 2007 erschienenen Roman „Heimsuchung“ beleuchtet die Schriftstellerin Jenny Erpenbeck anhand der Geschichte(n) des Hauses ihrer Großeltern am Scharmützelsee die deutsche Geschichte des 20. Jahrhunderts. Volker Schlöndorff hat das achronologisch erzählte Werk verfilmt.…
translated_excerpt_zh: 在她2007年出版的小说《家居寻找》中,作家珍妮·埃尔宾贝克(Jenny Erpenbeck)根据祖父母家(s)的故事(s)照亮了20世纪的德国历史。

解説・あらすじ

ベトナムで知られる都市伝説をモチーフに、怨霊が潜む屋敷に足を踏み入れたSNSインフルエンサーたちの運命を描いたホラー映画。 とあるSNSインフルエンサーのグループが、再生数を稼ぐため、ホア家の都市伝説にまつわる古い屋敷「ラウ・チュー・ホア」を訪れる。廃墟となったその場所でライブ配信を始める彼らだったが、開始直後から次々と超常現象が発生。やがてライブ配信は、彼らが「業を作り、業を返す」場へと変貌を遂げ、ホア家の令嬢の怨霊を前に1人また1人と恐怖の底に突き落とされていく。 本作が長編デビュー作となるベトナムの若手映画監督フン・チャンが、登場人物たちによるライブ配信という語り口で臨場感たっぷりに描き、本国ベトナムではSNSを中心に口コミで人気を集め大ヒットを記録した。

2026年製作／94分／ベトナム 原題または英題：Lầu Chú Hoả 配給：ニューゲーツ 劇場公開日：2026年10月30日
